utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to the New York City Council hearing, joint hearing for the Committee on Women and Gender Equity and the Committee on Criminal Justice.

chapters.summary: Farías identifies herself as Women and Gender Equity chair, welcomes Criminal Justice chair Brooks-Powers, and acknowledges Councilmembers Morano and Caban. She frames the hearing on maternal health and criminal justice.
chapters.title: Chair Farías welcomes attendees and introduces joint maternal health hearing

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Amanda Farias, Chair of the Committee on Women and Gender Equity.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'm excited to be joined by Chair of the Committee on Criminal Justice, Councilmember Silvina Brooks-Powers, for today's hearing on maternal health and criminal justice.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: First, I'd like to acknowledge my colleagues who are present, including Councilmembers Morano and Caban.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you both for being here today.

chapters.summary: Farías says women are the fastest-growing incarcerated group, three in four are childbearing age, and incarcerated pregnant people face barriers like inconsistent prenatal care and shackling. She notes Black and low-income women are disproportionately affected.
chapters.title: Chair Farías outlines maternal health crisis and racial disparities

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: The intersection of maternal health and the criminal justice system represents a critical public health and human rights crisis in the United States, where women are the fastest growing segment of the incarcerated population.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: National data shows that among incarcerated women, three out of four are of childbearing age.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Incarcerated pregnant individuals face severe systemic barriers, including inconsistent prenatal care, high rates of untreated substance use and mental health conditions, and the use of shackling during labor and delivery.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Whether an incarcerated pregnant person decides to carry their pregnancy to term or have an abortion, they have a constitutionally protected right to obtain appropriate medical care.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: It's important to note that mass incarceration and the maternal mortality crisis disproportionately impact black and low-income women.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Communities of color are disproportionately represented in New York City jail admissions, making up almost 90% of admissions, despite only compromising 52% of the city's general population.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: When compounded with the fact that black women overall are three times more likely

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: than white women to die because they were pregnant and three times more likely to suffer severe complications like fibroids, the added risks for black pregnant people of being incarcerated during pregnancy are high.

chapters.summary: Farías reports 52 incarcerated people were pregnant last year and describes gaps in mattresses, nutrition, outdoor time, safety, lactation support, and pregnancy education. She asks what CHS and DOC are doing to address these gaps.
chapters.title: Chair Farías cites NYC data on pregnant incarcerated people and gaps

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: In New York City, 52 incarcerated people were reported last year as pregnant by Correctional Health Services in a 2025 report produced by the Arnold Institute for Global Health.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: New York City's partnership interviews with individuals who gave birth while incarcerated in New York City revealed gaps in both the medical and correctional systems.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: The systems often lack mattresses sufficient for pregnancy support, nutritious foods, outdoor time and fresh air, safety from hazards such as mace and mold.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And supplies and support for lactation.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Participants also shared that they had limited access to the type of information about pregnancy and childbirth that would be available in the community, such as pamphlets, books, classes, and groups.

chapters.summary: Farías asks what correctional health services and DOC are doing to deliver maternal health services and invites Brooks-Powers to speak.
chapters.title: Chair Farías turns to Chair Brooks-Powers for opening statement

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So today, we'll ask what correctional health services and the Department of Correction are doing to address these gaps, and how are they delivering maternal health services to pregnant individuals while incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Now I'd like to invite Chair Brooks Powers to deliver her opening statement.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers welcomes everyone and says pregnancy, childbirth, and postpartum require medical care, nutrition, reproductive health care, and mental health support. These needs do not disappear upon incarceration.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers opens with need for consistent maternal care in custody

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Sylvina Brooks-Powers, Chair of the Committee on Criminal Justice.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I want to join Chair Fredias and welcome everyone to today's hearing on maternal health and criminal justice.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Pregnancy, childbirth, and postpartum period require consistent medical care, appropriate nutrition, access to reproductive health care,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: and support for both physical and mental health.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: These needs do not disappear when someone enters the criminal legal system.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Pregnant and postpartum people who are incarcerated need the same timely access to appropriate care to protect their health and the health of their children as any other New Yorker.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers says pregnant people in custody rely on providers and staff to identify pregnancies, coordinate appointments, respond to complications, and provide postpartum care. She stresses screening for perinatal mood and anxiety disorders.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers describes barriers to care and mental health needs

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: People who are pregnant while in custody face additional challenges in accessing health care.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: They rely on correctional health providers and facility staff to identify pregnancies, coordinate prenatal appointments, respond to medical complications, and provide care after delivery.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Interruptions in treatment, delays in referrals, or gaps in communication can have serious consequences.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Mental health needs also require attention throughout pregnancy and after childbirth, including screening for perinatal

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: mood and anxiety disorders and ensuring that people experiencing serious symptoms receive appropriate treatment.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers notes NYC has requirements for reporting pregnancy outcomes and prenatal/postnatal care, but asks how they work in practice. She wants to know how DOC and CHS coordinate care and whether people consistently receive services.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers questions implementation of NYC pregnancy requirements

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: New York City has taken steps to establish requirements and services for pregnant people in custody, including requirements related to reporting pregnancy outcomes and access to prenatal and postnatal care.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: However, it is important to understand how these requirements are implemented in practice.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How care is coordinated between the Department of Correction and Correctional Health Services, and whether people in custody are consistently receiving the services they need.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Today, the committee will examine how Correctional Health Services identifies and supports pregnant and postpartum people, including the procedures used during intake to identify pregnancy, recent childbirth, and breastfeeding.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The committee will also consider the health care needs of pregnant and postpartum people in the city's planned borough-based jail facilities.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: As the city develops these facilities, it is important to understand how their design, medical spaces, staffing, and service arrangements will accommodate pregnancy, childbirth recovery, breastfeeding, and the needs of parents and their infants.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers says the committee will consider how planned borough-based jails will accommodate pregnancy, childbirth recovery, breastfeeding, and parents with infants. She says planning requires clear procedures and resources for continuity of care.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers examines borough-based jail planning for maternal needs

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Planning for these needs requires more than providing medical space.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: It requires clear procedures and appropriate

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: resources to ensure continuity of care.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: This hearing will provide an opportunity to understand what data are available on pregnancy and maternal health care in custody, how the city monitors the quality and timelines of care, and what challenges remain in

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: ensuring that pregnant

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: and postpartum people receive appropriate treatment.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers lists Intro 902 by Councilmember Lee on mental health protocols and Resolutions 464, 497, and 498. She describes proposals on postpartum mental illness as a sentencing mitigator, prohibiting restraints, and postponing court proceedings.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers introduces Intro 902 and resolutions on postpartum sentencing and restraints

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: In addition to today's topic, the committee will be hearing introduction number 902, sponsored by Councilmember Lee, in relation to mental health protocols for pregnant and postpartum individuals in the custody of the Department of Correction.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We will also be hearing resolution number resolution numbers 467, 497 and 498.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The resolution 464 also sponsored by Councilmember Lee, but call on the state to pass legislation recognizing postpartum mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: As a mitigating factor in criminal sentencing.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Resolution 497, sponsored by Councilmember Hudson, would call on the state to pass Senate Bill 2667C and Assembly

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Bill 1670A, which would prohibit the use of restraints and limit other uses of force on pregnant and postpartum individuals.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: In the custody of law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Finally, Resolution 498, also sponsored by Councilmember Hudson, would call on the state to pass legislation

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: allowing pregnant people to postpone court proceedings when in the later stages of pregnancy.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: These pieces of legislation are meant to support pregnant people who have contact with

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The criminal legal system, a system where being pregnant or postpartum only amplifies the opportunity for trauma one can experience.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers thanks committee staff and her own staff, then says she looks forward to discussion with CHS, DOC, Board of Correction, advocates, and stakeholders. She turns the floor back to Chair Farías.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers thanks staff and stakeholders

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I would like to thank my staff and committee staff for their hard work, Jahari Frazier, counsel to the committee, Chad Benjamin, policy analyst, Casey Lasky, financial analyst, Owen Brady, my policy and budget director, and Renee Taylor, my chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I look forward to a productive discussion with the Correctional Health Services, the Department of Correction, the Board of Correction, advocates, and other stakeholders about the care available to pregnant and postpartum people in custody,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: the challenges they continue to face, and the steps needed to ensure that their medical and mental health needs are appropriately addressed.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Farias, and I will turn it back over to you.

chapters.summary: Farías says the committees will consider Intro 1144 by Councilmember Rita Joseph and others on gender-based violence analysis reporting. She also notes Intro 902 and Resolutions 464, 497, and 498.
chapters.title: Chair Farías introduces Intro 1144 and additional legislation

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Brooks-Powers.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Today, the committees will also consider the following legislation.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Intro number 1144, sponsored by Councilmember Rita Joseph, myself, and Councilmember Farrah Lewis, in relation to requiring a report regarding an analysis of gender-based violence in the city.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And as you've already heard from Chair Brooks-Powers, introductions 902, the committees also are considering resolutions numbers 464, 497, and 498.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Finally, I'd like to thank committee staff Julia Goldsmith-Pinkham, Katie Selina, and Ali Stauffer, as well as my own staff, Daniel Curtin, for all of their work on today's hearing.

chapters.title: Chair Farías gives witness slip and testimony instructions

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'd like to remind everyone who wishes to testify in person today that you must fill out a witness slip, which you can find on the desk of the Sergeant at Arms near the entrance of this room.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Please fill out a slip, even if you have already registered in advance, that you will be testifying in person today.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: If you wish to testify on any legislation, please indicate on the witness slip whether you're here to testify in favor of or in opposition to the legislation.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I also want to point out that we will not be voting on any legislation today.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: To allow as many people as possible to testify, the testimony will be limited to two minutes per person, whether you are testifying in person or on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'm also going to ask my colleagues to limit their questions and comments to five minutes.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Please note that witnesses who are here in person will testify before those who are signed into the Zoom webinar.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I will now turn it over to the committee counsel to administer the oath.

utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: In accordance with the rules of the council, I'll administer the affirmation to the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: I'll call on you each individually for a response.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please raise your right hands, including folks who may be called up to answer additional questions if you have more than four of you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

chapters.summary: Nancy Farias identifies herself as Chief of Nursing for NYC Health and Hospitals Correctional Health Services and introduces colleague Janette Merrill. She says CHS has been the direct physical and mental health provider for DOC custody since 2016.
chapters.title: CHS Chief of Nursing Nancy Farias introduces agency and patient population

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Brooks-Powers and Chair Farias and members of committees on criminal justice and on women and gender equity.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: My name is Nancy Farias and I serve as the Chief of Nursing for New York City Health and Hospitals Correctional Health Services.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: I am joined by my CHS colleague, Janette Merrill, Senior Assistant Vice President of Communications and External Affairs.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: We appreciate the opportunity to testify today on maternal health and criminal justice.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Since 2016, CHS has been the direct provider of physical and mental health services to people in the custody of New York City Department of Corrections, DOC.

chapters.summary: Farias says women are about 8% of CHS patients, with 82% enrolled in mental health services, 47% diagnosed with serious mental illness, and 34% with opioid use disorder. She notes 52 pregnant individuals were in CHS care last calendar year.
chapters.title: CHS reports high mental health and substance use needs among women in custody

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Women comprise about 8% of our patient population and have significant clinical and social medical needs.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Based on September 2026 data, 82% of the women in our care were enrolled in the mental health service.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: 47% of women were diagnosed with serious mental illness and 34% of women had an opioid use disorder.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: We recognize the tremendous responsibility and opportunity we have to provide high-quality health services, including perinatal.

chapters.summary: Farias says incarceration disrupts community care, so CHS conducts comprehensive medical evaluations at admission. At Rosie's, staff obtain reproductive health history and offer pregnancy testing to all reproductive-age patients, with referrals for follow-up.
chapters.title: CHS describes intake pregnancy screening and referrals

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Last calendar year, there were 52 pregnant individuals in total in our care.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: For many of our pregnant patients, their connections to community-based health care and support networks have been disrupted by their incarceration, making the services CHS provides especially important.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Other pregnant patients may have been out of care in the community due to challenges accessing providers or navigating services.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Presenting an opportunity to engage them in prenatal services that can promote maternal fetal health.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: CHS medical and nursing professionals conduct a comprehensive medical evaluation of all individuals when they are admitted to the New York City jail system.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: At the Rosem Singer Center, RMSC or ROSIES, clinical staff obtain a reproductive health history and offer pregnancy testing to all reproductive age patients.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Based on the information obtained during the intake assessment, patients may be referred for follow-up medical care or to the mental health service for additional evaluations.

chapters.summary: Farias says postpartum patients can see an OBGYN for postpartum or well-woman care. Pregnant patients receive prenatal labs, vitamins, on-site ultrasounds, education, and referrals to CHS and Elmhurst obstetricians.
chapters.title: CHS outlines prenatal and postpartum care at Rosie's and Elmhurst

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Postpartum patients can be referred to CHS's obstetrician for a postpartum visit or well-women care.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Which may include pelvic exam, pap smears, breast exams, or other reproductive and sexual health services.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: For patients who are pregnant at the time of jail admission, CHS clinicians order prenatal labs and vitamins and make referrals to the CHS obstetrician for prompt follow-up care.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Clinicians will work to obtain collateral information if the patient was engaged in care in the community.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: All pregnant patients receive routine prenatal care at Rosem Singer, where they have access to on-site ultrasounds as well as pregnancy-related education, including information about breastfeeding.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: A member of CHS's gender-related services team, which is part of CHS's reentry and transition services, will meet with the patient to offer additional support and information.

chapters.summary: Farias says patients with complex profiles receive care coordinated with Elmhurst Hospital, including joint telehealth visits and case conferences. Labor and delivery patients are transported to Elmhurst by FDNY EMS.
chapters.title: CHS details coordination with Elmhurst for complicated pregnancies

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Patients with more complicated clinical profiles also receive care in coordination with our colleagues at Elmhurst Hospital.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: To help orient all pregnant patients to the obstetric services available to them, CHS schedules joint introductory telehealth visits that include the patient, the CHS obstetrician, and the Elmhurst Hospital obstetrician.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Throughout the individual's pregnancy, our providers work closely with the labor and delivery and maternal fetal medicine providers at Umher's Hospital to coordinate care.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: At Elmhurst Hospital, our patients see a member of the hospital's care team who will be present should they deliver in custody.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: As previously mentioned, patients may also receive advanced prenatal testing and procedures at the hospital when clinically indicated.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: For both routine and high-risk pregnancies, CHS and Elmhurst medical providers conduct joint specific case conferences, which can also include clinicians from CHS's mental health service.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Patients who go into labor while incarcerated on Rikers Island are transported by FDNY EMS to Elmhurst Hospital for delivery.

chapters.summary: Farias says patients may apply to reside with infants in Rosie's Nursery, where CHS nurses provide clinical support. Mental health providers review history, interview patients, and develop treatment and reentry plans.
chapters.title: CHS describes Rosie's Nursery and mental health evaluation process

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Patients may apply through DOC's programs to care for and reside with their infants in the Rosie's Nursery, a housing area maintained by DOC with CHS's nurses providing clinical support to the new parents.

chapters.summary: Farias says CHS provides counseling, medication, and therapeutic housing, and clinicians assess trauma and perinatal mood disorders. Pregnant and postpartum patients with diagnosed mental health disorders are closely monitored.
chapters.title: CHS explains mental health services and perinatal screening

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: For patients who are referred for a mental health evaluation, a licensed CHS mental health provider reviews the patient's full mental health history, interviews the patient, and reviews an extensive social history with the patient.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: The information the mental health provider obtains during this assessment helps to inform their diagnostic determination, individualized treatment plan, case management, and reentry planning.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: The information also enables clinicians to assess clinical risk factors and to determine the patient's most appropriate treatment.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: appropriate mental health level of care.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: CHS provides a spectrum of jail-based mental health care that ranges from individual and group counseling and medication treatment to mental health therapeutic housing units for patients who have more robust mental health needs

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: and require increased clinical observation and care coordination.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: During all clinical encounters, mental health clinicians assess patients for trauma symptoms and mental health disorders, including perinatal mood and anxiety disorders and postpartum depression, as clinically indicated.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: All pregnant and postpartum patients with diagnosed mental health disorders are closely monitored by CHS's mental health service.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Should a pregnant or postpartum patient require a higher level of psychiatric care than can be provided on writers, the patient will be referred to Elmhurst Hospital in coordination with CHS and hospital leadership.

chapters.summary: Farias says many pregnant patients have complex comorbidities requiring robust care coordination. CHS reentry staff connect patients to community resources, Medicaid, housing, and Elmhurst social workers for follow-up.
chapters.title: CHS describes reentry and discharge planning for pregnant and postpartum patients

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Many of our pregnant patients have complex medical and psychiatric comorbidities and require robust care coordination and treatment plans.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: CHS's Reentry and Transition Service helps connect patients to clinical resources in the community to help ensure continuity of care upon discharge from jail.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: All pregnant and postpartum patients and all patients receiving mental health services receive an individualized discharge plan in addition to the core reentry services available to all patients.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Which includes assistance applying for Medicaid.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: CSS reentry staff coordinate with DOC and their contracted vendors to support transition planning as appropriate, including referrals to housing.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: In addition, Elmhurst Hospital obtains contact information for all pregnant patients and hospital social workers are available to support delivery plans and follow-up care after release from jail.

chapters.summary: Farias says Intro 902 would require protocols for identifying, screening, referring, monitoring, and following up pregnant and postpartum individuals with mental health needs. CHS says it is the appropriate agency but wants language refined to avoid legislating clinical decision-making.
chapters.title: CHS comments on Intro 902 and concerns about clinical decision-making

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Intro 902 would require the establishment of protocols governing the identification, screening, referral, monitoring, and follow-up care of pregnant individuals

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: and postpartum individuals in DOC custody who have or may have mental health needs.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: As written, the bill would require DOC to establish and maintain these protocols.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: But CHS is the direct and independent provider of medical and mental health services to people in DOC custody and will serve as the appropriate agency.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: The protocols outlined in the legislation largely align with current CHS practices as they relate to referrals to care, mental health screenings, psychiatric evaluations, clinical documentation, and discharge planning.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: However, we would want to refine the language to ensure the bill doesn't legislate clinical decision-making and ensures that CHS can continue to provide care in accordance with the most current and appropriate standards of care and clinical practice.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: We would like to discuss with Council the provision of the bill that would require CHS to establish procedures

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: for identifying postpartum status when an individual does not proactively disclose such status.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: CHS providers work to establish a relationship of trust with our patients, which can prove more challenging in a carceral setting.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: All of the services we provide are voluntary.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: And we respect every patient's right to engage in clinical services and to provide personal information as the individual feels comfortable doing so.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: We would therefore appreciate the opportunity to better understand the intention of the Council relative to this specific provision and to explore ways to address any concerns without

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: jeopardizing the sanctity of the provider-patient relationship and while protecting the privacy and rights of the patient.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Thank you and we look forward to answering your questions.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: You will now hear a testimony from our colleagues at the O.C.

chapters.summary: Valerie Greysock identifies herself as Assistant Commissioner in the Division of Programs and Community Partnerships. She says CHS provides medical and mental health care while DOC facilitates access through appointments, transportation, referrals, and accommodations.
chapters.title: DOC Assistant Commissioner Valerie Greysock introduces DOC role

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Brooks Powers and Chair Fadillas and members of the committees.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: My name is Valerie Graysock and I'm an Assistant Commissioner within the Division of Programs and Community Partnerships.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to discuss the New York City Department of Corrections support for pregnant and postpartum women in our care.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: As our colleagues at Correctional Health Services have described, CHS provides medical and mental health care within the jails, while DOC facilitates access to that care through appointments, transportation, referrals, and necessary accommodations.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Our responsibility also includes supporting individuals in our care

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: as they prepare for childbirth, recover following pregnancy outcome, and care for their children.

chapters.summary: Greysock says DOC offers doula services at Rosie's through the Caribbean Women's Health Association. Doulas provide birth planning, breastfeeding education, newborn care, and pregnancy loss support twice weekly, serving 20 women and over 400 hours from January to June.
chapters.title: DOC describes doula services through Caribbean Women's Health Association

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Through our partnership with the Caribbean Women's Health Association, the DOC offers doula services to individuals housed at Rose M.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Singer Center.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Doulas provide non-medical, physical, emotional, and informational support, including birth planning, breastfeeding education, newborn care, and support following pregnancy loss.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Services are offered twice weekly with labor and delivery support.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: available upon request.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: From January through June of this year, the program served 20 women and provided over 400 hours of support.

chapters.summary: Greysock says DOC operates a residential nursery where eligible mothers can stay with infants until the child's first birthday. Participation is voluntary, admission considers the child's best interest, and an early education counselor helps mothers.
chapters.title: DOC describes residential nursery program at Rosie's

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: DOC also operates a residential nursery at RMSC where eligible mothers can remain with their infants until the child's first birthday.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Participation in the nursery program is completely voluntary.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Not all individuals who are eligible want to participate, and admission decisions consider the best interest of the child.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: The program supports early bonding and parental care with an early educational counselor helping mothers meet their baby's needs.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: We recognize that pregnancy and early parenthood can be especially difficult during incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: These programs help women in our care access practical guidance, personal support, and opportunities to build and maintain their relationships with their children during a very difficult time.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: And we're proud to offer them.

chapters.summary: Greysock says pregnancy and early parenthood are difficult during incarceration and the programs offer guidance, support, and bonding opportunities. She thanks the committees and welcomes questions.
chapters.title: DOC concludes testimony on pregnancy and parenting programs

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to share about these important services, and we welcome your questions.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'll now turn it over to Public Advocate Jumaane Williams for his remarks.

chapters.summary: Williams thanks the chairs and says pregnancy, childbirth, and postpartum needs do not change when a person is incarcerated. He says people in custody must receive timely medical care, mental health support, and dignity.
chapters.title: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams begins testimony on incarcerated pregnancy

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Morning, as mentioned, my name is Jumaane Williams, Public Advocate for the City of New York.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I want to thank Chair Farias and Chair Brooks-Powers and members of the Women and Gender Equity and Criminal Justice Committees for holding this important hearing and for the opportunity to share testimony.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Pregnancy, childbirth, and the post-mortem.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: modern period are significantly physically and mentally demanding, and those needs do not change in any way when a pregnant person is incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Those in custody must be able to access timely, appropriate medical care, receive necessary mental health support, and be treated with dignity throughout pregnancy, childbirth, and the postmodern period.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, ACOG, in particular, have emphasized the importance of incarcerated individuals receiving high-quality, trauma-informed, and comprehensive medical care.

chapters.summary: Williams cites ACOG guidance and says incarcerated pregnant people often face inadequate care, delayed obstetric responses, isolation during delivery, and shackling. He notes post-delivery separation increases postpartum depression risks.
chapters.title: Williams describes systemic gaps and dehumanizing treatment in correctional facilities

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Unfortunately, incarcerated pregnant persons frequently do not receive adequate care due to systemic gaps and harsh, sometimes barely humane conditions across correctional systems.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Pregnant and postpartum individuals often face a variety of medical and emotional challenges, including complications during pregnancy.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The physical demands of childbirth and mental health conditions that emerge are worsened during pregnancy or after delivery.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: These conditions are often exacerbated by the failure of many jails and prisons to provide full access to medications for opioid use disorders or the abrupt stoppage of treatment.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Postpartum, increasing overdose risks.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Dehumanizing treatment reported by incarcerated pregnant people, including inadequate prenatal monitoring, delayed responses to obstetric symptoms, isolation during delivery, and the traumatic use of shackles during labor, a practice banned in New York in 2009.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In addition, the rapid post-delivery separation from newborns remains a deeply distressing reality in most facilities and has led to increased rates of post-mortem depression.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: These concerns are particularly important in correction of safety.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: where individuals must rely on the facility to access care.

chapters.summary: Williams says Intro 902 would require DOC and CHS to establish written protocols for pregnant and postpartum individuals with mental health needs. He also supports resolutions to postpone court proceedings and prohibit restraints during labor and interrogation.
chapters.title: Williams supports Intro 902 and Resolutions 497 and 498

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Today, the council is hearing intro 902 by Councilmember Lee, which will require the Department of Corrections and coordination with the correctional

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: health services to establish and maintain written protocols related to identification, screening, referral, monitoring, and follow-up of pregnant and postpartum individuals with mental health needs.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: These specific protocols will be made public, available, and shared with all staff involved in their care.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This would address the importance of keeping a reference point so that all health concerns can be properly addressed.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It is imperative that these protocols support timely referrals, appropriate psychiatric evaluations, and establish coordination between medical and mental health providers.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: There must be procedures to help individuals maintain access to medications or support services as they transition out of a facility.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The council will also hear Reso 498 by Councilmember Hudson, which calls on the state legislature to pass and the governor to sign legislation to postpone court proceedings as requested by individuals in the later stages of pregnancy.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Court appearances often involve transportation, arraignment processing, and prolonged waiting, which often proposes substantial burdens on individuals who are also

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: close to birth, which can often lead to deeply disturbing incidents in the courtroom akin to what happened in May with Samantha Randazzo, who gave birth while shackled in a courtroom in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Reso 497 also by Councilman Hudson will call on the state to pass and governor to sign a bill in relation to prohibiting the use of restraints in incarcerated individuals during labor, absent extraordinary circumstances, and on pregnant persons during custodial interrogation.

chapters.summary: Williams says no one should be shackled during vulnerable medical moments and cites incidents involving Samantha Randazzo and Luz Burke. He notes Black and brown women are disproportionately affected and asks about continuity of care.
chapters.title: Williams calls for dignity and racial equity in maternal care

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It is important that no individual should be shackled during deeply vulnerable medical critical moment.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The safety, dignity, and peace will give birth most, while giving birth must be paramount.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It is essential that what happened to Luz Burke, who was put in full body restraints while she was pregnant and retained in Rikers Island, does not happen to anyone.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: These proposals raise broader concerns about the legal system.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Accommodates pregnancy and recovery.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We must ensure that staff and health providers fully understood that responsibilities of the medical needs are addressed properly.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We must also ensure that decisions about court appearances and custody does not needlessly interfere with continuing care.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Looking forward to the administration hearing from them about how it's ensuring timely and equitable maternal health care for pregnant and post-mortem individuals in custody.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: What procedures are in place to maintain continuity of care as those in custody are transferred across facilities and how the city can further help in ensuring all people receive adequate care pre and post-mortem.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I have to mention that obviously when we hear these stories, it's usually black and brown women who are going through this.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I'd be remiss if I didn't mention that.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Unfortunately, usually the case.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you for this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony, Public Advocate Williams.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'd now like to invite Councilmember Hudson to give remarks about her resolutions.

chapters.summary: Hudson describes a pregnant woman who went into labor while handcuffed in Brooklyn Criminal Court. Resolution 497 would prohibit restraints during labor, delivery, postpartum recovery, and custodial interrogations; Resolution 498 would allow postponement of court proceedings in late pregnancy.
chapters.title: Council Member Hudson introduces Resolutions 497 and 498

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chairs, for the opportunity to speak on two resolutions that this committee is hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Earlier this year, New Yorkers were confronted with the deeply troubling news of a pregnant woman who went into labor while handcuffed and awaiting arraignment in Brooklyn Criminal Court.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: That incident raised urgent...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: questions about how our justice system treats pregnant people.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Resolution 497 calls on the state to pass legislation prohibiting the use of restraints on incarcerated individuals during labor, delivery, and postpartum recovery, and extends protections to pregnant people during custodial interrogations.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Childbirth requires the ability to respond to rapidly changing circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Restraints put both

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: the person giving birth and their child at risk.

chapters.summary: Hudson says no one should choose between health and navigating the criminal legal system, and temporary postponement does not end accountability. She urges the state legislature and governor to pass the protections.
chapters.title: Hudson urges passage of protections for pregnant people in court

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Resolution 498 calls on the state to pass legislation allowing court proceedings to be postponed at the request of individuals in the later stages of pregnancy.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: No one should have to choose between protecting their health during pregnancy and navigating the demands of the criminal legal system.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: A temporary postponement can provide the time needed for childbirth and recovery without ending a case or eliminating accountability.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: No one should be shackled in labor.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: No one should be forced into a courtroom days before giving birth, not for any charge, not for any reason.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We have an opportunity to close gaps in our laws and ensure that pregnant New Yorkers are treated with the care and respect their circumstances require.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I urge the state legislature to pass these protections and the governor to sign them into law because dignity does not end at the courthouse door.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Hudson.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'll now jump right into questions.

chapters.summary: Farías asks when individuals are screened for pregnancy. Jeanette Merrill says all new admissions receive comprehensive medical evaluations, and women of reproductive age at Rosie's receive pregnancy testing with referrals to CHS OBGYN.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks CHS about intake pregnancy screening and staff training

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: At what points during intake and detention are individuals screened for pregnancy?

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So I'm Jeanette Merrill, Correctional Health Services.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So as part of the routine new admissions process, everyone who comes to Rikers receives a comprehensive medical evaluation conducted by our nursing and medical staff.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So at Rosie's, that includes for all women of reproductive age, pregnancy testing.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: And then women who are found to be pregnant are scheduled with the CHS OBGYN for additional examinations.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, and who's conducting the pregnancy screenings and what trainings do they receive beforehand?

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So that would be our nursing staff.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: So actually our patients receive three levels of screening.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Or a first individual that they'll encounter will be a patient care associate who will be the one who does the point of care testing and will be then doing the urine screening with the urine dipstick.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: And then they subsequently see a person of a higher license to complete their intake, which would be a registered nurse and also followed up by a nurse practitioner or MDPA.

chapters.summary: Farías asks whether nurses are DOC or CHS staff and how medical emergencies are handled. Nancy Farias says CHS staff conduct intake and respond first to housing units, stabilizing patients and escalating as clinically needed.
chapters.title: Chair Farías questions CHS staffing and emergency response protocols

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And are the registered nurses and the nurse practitioners hired by DOC, or are they?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: They're correctional health services.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Correctional health services, sorry, and their regular staff there at Rikers, or are they per diem by any chance?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Well, we have persons who are hired specifically to work at Rosenstein.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And, you know, there are obviously many potential possible complications during pregnancy.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: What's the protocol when someone experiences a medical emergency?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: So as all our patients, a medical emergency is initiated at the housing level where the individual is at, and we coordinate with the Department of Corrections to facilitate response to the unit.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Correctional Health Services are the first responders to the unit to assess and stabilize the patient, and then we would escalate based on the clinical assessment of the patient at the time.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, and are staff trained to recognize warning signs like vaginal bleeding, contractions, fluid leakage, severe abdominal pain, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Yes.

chapters.summary: Farías asks whether DOC follows the administrative code minimum of twice-weekly doula services for four hours with two doulas. Greysock says the Caribbean Women's Health Association is on site at least twice weekly for four hours.
chapters.title: Chair Farías questions DOC on doula service frequency and staffing

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, and then in terms of the administrative code requiring that doula services be provided,

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: at a frequency of at least twice a week for four hours with at least two doulas available.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Does DOC follow this minimum or does it provide greater access to doula services than that?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Yes, we have a wonderful partnership with the Women's Caribbean Health Association, and they are at Rosen Singer at least twice a week for four hours each day.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, and how many doulas currently provide services to people in custody at DOC?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Two doulas.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Two doulas.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And just give me there how many days per week they're available, usual hours of availability.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: They're typically on site twice a week for at least four hours, sometimes longer.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Farías notes doula service hours rose to 426 hours from January to June 2026 and 438 hours from July to December 2025, compared with 148 hours in early 2025. Greysock attributes this to demand and doulas sometimes coming a third day.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks about jump in doula service hours

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: There was a massive jump in service hours provided by doulas in the last two reporting periods compared to before with doulas providing 426 service hours from January to June of 2026

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: and 438 service hours from July to December of 2025 as compared to 148 service hours for January to June of 2025.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Is there a specific reason that doulas were able to provide so much more service over the past 12 months?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: I think dual services are very important and very valued by the individual in our care.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Although the minimum is two days a week, oftentimes they do come on the third day because the women often ask for them.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: They're often kind of like their main go-to, and they really serve as a source of important emotional support.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: So I've found that they often come additional hours.

chapters.summary: Farías asks if doulas are compensated for extra hours. Greysock says yes through a DOC contract with the Caribbean Women's Health Association, which has been renewed and may be expanded.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks about doula compensation and contract

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Are they compensated for those hours?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Yes, we have a contract with the vendor.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And what organization or what vendor is contracted for dual services currently?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: It's an organization called Caribbean Women's Health Association.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: They've been a wonderful partner since the beginning.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And that contract is through DOC or CHS?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: It's the contract through DOC.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: DOC.

chapters.summary: Farías asks how long DOC has had the doula contract and whether it is open for RFP. Greysock says the contract has been renewed for several years, originally two years and currently one year, following procurement rules.
chapters.title: Chair Farías questions duration and procurement of doula contract

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: How long have we had that contract?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Is there like an open RFP, RFA, or have we had it for an extended time period?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: We've had it for at least several years.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: We've been renewing it.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: The original contract for two years and the current contract is for one year.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: But every year we renew this contract and we're actually looking to increase our investment in dual programming because the feedback has been overwhelmingly positive.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Sorry, just for my own clarification, is typically the contract for two years or is it one year with option to renew for an additional?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: The current one is for one year.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: For one year.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Have there been any other vendors that we've used in the past with DOC for doula services that's provided to folks that are incarcerated?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: So we follow the procurement rules when we release the solicitation, and this vendor has been selected during this period and the previous period

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: based on their extensive experience working in the city and with women and with justice-involved women.

chapters.summary: Farías asks when doula services started and whether they serve only Rosie's. Greysock says services began when the law took effect and the contract covers anyone pregnant or postpartum, though services typically occur at Rosie's.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks when DOC began doula services and which facilities are covered

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Remind me again, when did we start providing doula services at DOC?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: We started the year that the law went into effect.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And how many facilities can the doulas access, or is it just for Rosie's?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: So their contract is to serve anyone in our care who is pregnant.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: So they typically facilitate services at Rosem Singer, but the goal is for them to be able to serve anyone who is pregnant or postpartum.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And that's in the contract.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Yes.

chapters.summary: Farías asks how doulas enter DOC facilities. Greysock says contracted providers and volunteers go through a volunteer ID process, allowing them to access the nursery or housing areas to meet women.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks about doula facility access process

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, and can someone walk me through the process that a doula has to follow to enter the DOC facility?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Is it like a person from the public, or are they a staff member?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: For all of our contracted providers and volunteers, there's a volunteer ID process.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: The doulas submit a volunteer ID application.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Once they receive an ID, they have an ID that allows them to access the facility.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: So they can go directly to the nursery or to any other housing area to meet with women where they are.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Farías asks what happens if a pregnancy is reported after intake. Merrill says the patient is referred to CHS OBGYN, prenatal vitamins and labs are ordered, and care is coordinated with Elmhurst.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks about pregnancy reported after intake

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And then for procedures around individual reports for possible, what procedures are followed from folks when an individual reports a possible pregnancy after intake?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Let's say we did not catch it.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: They would go through the same process.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: It would still be a referral to our CHS, OBGYN.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: We would order prenatal vitamins and labs and then potentially coordinate with Elmhurst Hospital.

chapters.summary: Farías asks how many pregnant people missed scheduled prenatal or obstetric appointments because DOC did not produce them. Merrill reports non-production rates for on-island and off-island appointments across calendar years 2023, 2024, and 2025.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks about missed prenatal appointments due to non-production

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, and in the past three calendar years, how many pregnant people in DOC's custody missed scheduled prenatal or obstetric appointments because they were not produced by DOC?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And if you can possibly, if we have those by year, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So in calendar year 25, 53% of on-island obstetric appointments were non-productions.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: But I should note that is the initially scheduled appointment.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: If an individual misses that first scheduled appointment, we coordinate to reschedule and then can always escalate as needed at the local level to ensure the woman has access to care.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So again, 53% non-production for on-island and then off-island, meaning Elmhurst Hospital, is 40% non-production.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: And then calendar year 24, on island, 37% non-production, 43% for off island.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: And then calendar year 23, on island, 27% non-production, 69% off island non-production.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Got it.

chapters.summary: Farías asks how many people in DOC custody were transported for labor, delivery, or pregnancy-related emergencies. Merrill says 15 individuals gave birth in custody in 2023 and 2025 and were transported to Elmhurst.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks about hospital transports for labor and pregnancy emergencies

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And in each of these three calendars, how many people in DOC custody were transported to a hospital for labor and delivery or a pregnancy-related emergency?

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So fortunately, very few women are still in custody at the time that they deliver.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: 2023 and 2025, there were 15 individuals who gave birth while in custody and would have been transported to Elmhurst for labor and delivery.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Farías asks how many restraint incidents involving pregnant or postpartum people were recorded. Chelsea Chard says there have been zero reported incidents in the past three years, and explains DOC policy limits restraints to absolute last resort.
chapters.title: Chair Farías questions zero reported restraint incidents on pregnant people

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And how many of these incidents were involving the use of restraints on pregnant or postpartum people in DOC custody were recorded?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Good morning, Chelsea Chard, Senior Advisor.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: We have zero reported incidents within the past three years.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Is there a reason why we have zero reported when we know of at least?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: One case where we have zero recorded period of no restraints being utilized, despite some of the records that folks are giving to us as,

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to speak to those individual cases.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: It is our policy that in the case that DOC knows that an individual is pregnant or eight weeks postpartum, restraints are to be used only as an absolute last resort.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: And in the case that restraints are used, a report is generated, a positive report is generated to our state oversight body, and we don't have any of those reports for the past three years.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Can you give me an idea of how that process works?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Like who's in the room when there's potential use of restraint and who has to elevate that or generate that report?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: So generally it would be the staff who are with that person, whether it's during transportation or kind of wherever they might be within a facility or a clinic setting.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Again, the goal is to never have to use restraints.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: There is a lot of de-escalation and work that happens with that person, whether it's from DOC staff or other staff who might be present in the room.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: In the case that there is imminent risk of harm to the person or to others, that would be really the only case, and that is, again, exceptional and rare.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: And in those cases, only front restraints are used.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: And the person who is applying the restraints is the one who is submitting that report within one business day.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'm going to now pass it over to Chair Brooks Powers for her questions.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair, and thank you for the testimony.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Again, it's always helpful if we can get the testimony in advance.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So my hope is that I'm not redundant in some of the questions that I'm asking.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how medical information is shared between NYPD and DOC when custody changes. Chard says NYPD does not share medical information with DOC and people go through medical screening at the courthouse.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers asks how NYPD and DOC share pregnancy information

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Going back to screenings for pregnancy, postpartum status, how is medical information shared between NYPD and DLC when someone changes custody?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Sorry, that's between NYPD and...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Department of Correction.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How is medical information shared between NYPD and DLC when someone changes custody?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So when they're going from being in custody with the NYPD, they're being transferred over to the Department of Correction to be in custody.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How is that information shared for an individual that is pregnant?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: NYPD doesn't share medical information with us.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: They would go through the medical screenings that are happening at the courthouse.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But is there any documentation or anything to denote, like, this person in custody is pregnant or any type of dynamic related to that condition?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks if pregnancy and postpartum screenings occur only at intake. Merrill says screenings occur primarily at intake but can be repeated as clinically indicated, including at subsequent clinic appointments.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers asks whether pregnancy screenings are repeated during detention

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Are pregnancy and postpartum screenings conducted only at intake, or are they repeated during detention?

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So it would be as clinically indicated.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: Primarily it would occur at intake, but of course patients have the right to refuse services as well, so a subsequent clinic appointment could address perinatal needs.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So they're offered even beyond intake?

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What procedures are followed when an individual reports a possible pregnancy after intake?

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So at that point, the individual would be referred to the CHS, OBGYN.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: We would order labs, vitamins, and then start the coordination process with Elmhurst Hospital.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how DOC ensures CHS is promptly notified when someone is identified as pregnant. Chard says intake screening is done by CHS, and DOC generally does not hold medical information or require disclosure.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers asks how DOC ensures CHS is notified of pregnancy

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And how does the department ensure that CHS is promptly notified when a person is identified as pregnant or postpartum?

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So CHS would identify a patient as pregnant or postpartum, and then according to New York State correction law, a woman or patient who is within eight weeks of a pregnancy event, that information is shared with DOC.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But in terms of DOC, how are they ensuring that CHS is promptly notified when a person is identified as being pregnant?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Because they're coming into care first at Department of Correction, correct?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Pregnant.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: So someone would, when someone's coming in through intake, the first step that they're doing once they're on Rikers Island is going through that intake screening process.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And the intake is done by CHS?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: There's generally not a case where DOC would be notifying CHS.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: It would be occurring the other way around because we don't hold that medical information and we don't require people to disclose to us.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Got it.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks for the racial demographic breakdown of pregnant people in DOC custody over three years. Merrill says CHS does not collect racial demographic information, though most women in care are Black and brown and all pregnancies are treated as higher risk.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers asks for racial demographics of pregnant people in custody

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What is the racial demographic breakdown of pregnant people in Department of Correction custody over the last three calendar years?

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So CHS doesn't collect racial demographic information, although if it's clinically indicated, we would seek that from the patient.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: We do know, it was mentioned in testimony, that the majority of women in our care are black and brown women.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: Black women in particular have higher risks of pregnancy and childbirth-related incidents.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So really we're treating every pregnancy by nature of the woman and the patient being in custody as higher risk.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So we're not stratifying by race in that way.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks where the nursery is located and its capacity. Greysock says it is at Rosie's with maximum occupancy of about 15 rooms for mothers and children, and mothers can keep infants overnight.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers questions nursery location and capacity

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Going over to the nursery program.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Where is the nursery located within the Department of Correction system?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: The nursery is located within the Rose M.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Singh Center.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And how many beds and cribs are available, and what is the maximum occupancy?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: The maximum occupancy is about 15.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: 15 rooms for a mom and also children.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Are mothers able to keep their infants with them throughout the day and overnight?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What is the current operational status of the Department of Correction nursery program?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: We are proud to offer one of the country's oldest correctional nurseries.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: So the nursery is fully operational.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: We have a mom currently inside the program.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: We have a wonderful partnership with Caribbean Women's Health Association, as I mentioned earlier, to provide doula services and help mom around newborn care, emotional support, and recovery after childbirth.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: We also have wonderful partnerships with our children, which provides reentry support inside the nursery.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: And, you know, it's really designed to look and feel like a nursery.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: There are cribs and children's toys and books and a rocking chair for the mom.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: It's really kind of designed to support the care of the mom and the child.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: And actually last year,

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: completely renovated the nursery and purchased all new furniture, new cribs, new toys, new books.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
