utterances.text: We painted the walls, we did the floors, all with the goal of making sure that it's a welcoming and warm environment for the mom and the baby.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks if there are enough nursery slots for every birthing person. Greysock says yes, but currently only one mother and infant are in the nursery while other pregnant individuals remain in general population.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers asks about nursery slots and housing pregnant people

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Are there enough slots for every birthing person in Department of Correction custody to avail themselves of the nursery?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I know you mentioned just now that there was a mother right now in the program.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Is there only one person that...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Either has an infant or that is pregnant right now in custody?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: There's currently one mom and an infant in the nursery.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: There are other individuals who are pregnant.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And so are they located still in general population?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Because with my last visit, I raised concerns about that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I know Commissioner had mentioned that effective that day, they would be moving those in custody that are pregnant into the nursery for safety reasons.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Nell Colon.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: I'm the Deputy Commissioner of Programs and Community Partnerships, and I was on that visit.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: I just want to emphasize that while there is only one individual in the nursery right now with their child, all of the women who are pregnant actually after that visit have been afforded and offered the opportunity to move into the nursery.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: It is a voluntary move, but we have been ensuring that the application is presented and that they are given the opportunity to apply, and we currently have an application pending.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So they have to apply to be moved there?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Can you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: So in order to move into the nursery, a screening does occur.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Part of it is with medical and mental health, but notably it also is with the administration of children's services.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: So taking into account of any cases of child abuse or neglect that may be indicated by ACS.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: And with that, those two pieces of information are then reviewed by the department.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: And very often, if cleared, they would be moving into the nursery.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And only one of the pregnant moms have applied and the rest have refused?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Well, the program is voluntary, and we also have a transient population, so we might have had someone who was pregnant last week, and then they might have been released.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: And so everyone who is pregnant who is in our care now is offered the application.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Some of the moms chose not to complete the application, and we currently have one pending.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Do we have an idea of why they refused?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: I think a lot of times they anticipate being released before giving birth.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks what supports are available to parents and children in the nursery. Greysock describes doulas, social workers, correctional counselors, Our Children reentry support, and partnerships with WPA, Osborne, New Hour, and Homebase.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers asks about supports in the nursery program

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What supports are available to parents and children in the nursery program?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: So the doulas are on site at least twice a week, and they help the mom around newborn care, anything from diapering, breastfeeding, any kind of emotional support that's needed.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: We also have a team of counselors that are regularly inside the nursery.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: So we have a social worker and a correctional counselor that provides one-on-one support, coordination with other programs, coordination with CHS, assistance with any paperwork.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: They're sort of the main go-to for any kind of key DOC services.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Our Children has a presence in the nursery as well.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: They primarily support around reentry, and they also coordinate with a network of other nonprofits that have a presence at Rosen Singer Centers.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: That includes the Women's Prison Association, Osborne Association, New Hour, and Homebase.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: There are other services that are available as well, for example, chaplaincy and, of course, any mandated services.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: We also have an early childhood education counselor who is at the nursery providing support as well.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks where nursery eligibility notices are posted and how the application process works. Merrill says the gender-related services team meets with every pregnant person and facilitates applications.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers asks about nursery notices and application process

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Going back to your statement about the application process, are notices regarding the nursery and potential

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: eligibility posted anywhere besides the clinic?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And if so, where are they posted?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: I believe they're posted in intake as well.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: I would also note our gender-related services team meets with every pregnant individual in custody, and part of the work they're doing is facilitating access to nurse grade applications.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What's the longest someone can remain in the nursery?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: So with a child, you can remain up to one year.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: That's not including, obviously, during the pregnancy time period.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: When children age out of the nursery program, has the Department of Correction noticed any negative effects on the parent if the parent remains incarcerated?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: What I can say is our DOC program staff and the doulas work very closely with the mom to support her coming up to that time.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: We've even had a birthday for the child, a first birthday.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: So there's a lot of counseling and support because we recognize.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: That being a new mom can be difficult when incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: And as part of the postpartum visit, there are mental health screening questions if the woman weren't already enrolled in the mental health service.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: And we do have a very low threshold for those referrals.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how DOC plans to house women and gender expansive people after Rikers closes. Nell Colon says Queens Detention Center is being considered, and Brooks-Powers questions limiting women to one borough.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers questions borough-based jail plans for women

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Just pivoting to borough-based jails.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What is the Department of Correction's current plan for housing women and gender expansive people after Riker's Island closes?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: I think there's a few things that are being explored right now for how we're supporting both women and gender expansive people after Rikers.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: At this time, I believe there are plans for us to consider the Queens Detention Center, although I think other options are being looked into right now.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: That's good to know because the current plan states that there will be 450 beds for women and gender expansive people at the Queensborough Base Jail.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And one, I'm curious as to how we came to that number and two, why are we limiting the location for women to one location, considering that majority of the women that are in custody are often the caregivers in their household,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: placing a burden on them when the men are in their respective boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So I'm just curious how we decided that the women had to be in one borough.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a good question because it's been a lot of planning, and I think there has been some conversation back and forth as we've solicited community feedback.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: I believe most of the...

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Numbers that we were talking about in terms of bed space were based on previous projections as, you know, kind of years ago these were coming to fruition.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: And my understanding is similar to sort of how we operate on Rikers.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: We recognize that when we have certain populations, they need specialized services.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: And in order to offer those specialized services, it can be helpful to have them all in one location so that all those services can kind of be hubbed in that location as well.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: I believe that was part of the thinking in terms of designing it in that manner.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How many women are in custody now, today?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Give me one second.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay, so not far from the 450.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Is there an opportunity to revisit having women in just one location?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Well, I would say I think there is an opportunity for us to consider a variety of ways that we can support women before they even come into our custody.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: And so I think the city is open to these conversations.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But to be clear, in terms of the construction and the design of the four borough-based jails, is there still an opportunity?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: To accommodate women at more than just the Queens location?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Quite honestly, we'd have to get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I would greatly appreciate if we could explore that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I think that it is problematic that we only place the women in one, and I've been saying this from the moment it was announced, quite honestly.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: As chair now, I want to be able to work with the administration to try to work through that because we do have folks that whether they're pregnant, they may have kids at home, it just places an extra barrier when

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: the whole...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Idea behind these borough base included having people being connected to community.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: and connected to family.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So I think that it's a bit unfair that we're now saying, okay, accept the women.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Because they require different levels of care.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I think it's the obligation and the responsibility of the Department of Corrections to ensure that no matter where they are, that they're getting that care.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks for DOC's written policy governing restraints on pregnant people. Chard says policy aligns with state guidelines, emphasizes de-escalation, and permits front restraints only as a last resort for imminent harm.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers asks about written restraint policy for pregnant people

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Restraints.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What is the Department of Correction current written policy governing restraints on pregnant people?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Our current policy is in alignment with state guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: And so I think, as I had said previously, the goal is never to use restraints on an individual who is either pregnant or eight weeks postpartum.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: In the case that someone is having a challenging time, which, of course, this is a hard time to be pregnant there in jail.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: There is, the training is essentially what we would want for any avoidance of, you know, using restraints, which is a lot of de-escalation, a lot of talking with the person.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: You know, I think a lot of our staff have rapport with folks.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: And so in moments when someone's upset or they're getting escalated in some way, there is an emphasis on de-escalating and trying to calm the person down for however long that takes.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: And really only in the case that someone is essentially coming to the point of self-harm and imminent risk of harming themselves is when we would consider using restraints.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: And the only restraints that are to be used are in

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: front of the body and we remove those as soon as the person is calmed down.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: We don't wait to get to any particular location.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: So in the case they need to be used, they're used for as short of a duration as possible.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: And then as I mentioned, there is a report that's generated following that.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: And in the case that restraints are used, the woman is also escorted to clinic or otherwise does receive a medical follow-up after that incident.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The chair is going to have some more questions around that.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers revisits a September 23 hearing where General Counsel Conroy said deadlocking was not occurring, while Legal Aid testified clients were deadlocked. Chard says DOC cannot comment on ongoing litigation but maintains its prior position.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers follows up on deadlocking allegations

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I just wanted to pivot really quickly for the Department of Correction regarding deadlocking.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: This is a follow-up from our September 23rd hearing.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So at the committee on criminal justice hearing on September 23rd, I asked...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: General Counsel Conroy to confirm that deadlocking is no longer occurring.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: He responded that it was not, referencing the DOI, that DOI was unable to substantiate claims about deadlocking from 2024.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Later in the same hearing, Barbara Hamilton of Legal Aid testified that multiple clients have been deadlocked this year.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Allegations which DOC was surely aware of due to ongoing litigation.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Should we understand your previous testimony to mean that those allegations are false?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: So we can't speak to any of the specific allegations that were made since there's ongoing litigation and legal action.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: But I do believe that our position remains what the general counsel stated in that hearing.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But are you acknowledging that you're aware that litigation is going on right now?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: I don't work in the legal division, but I believe there are some legal proceedings related to lock-in, but we can't comment on those specifically.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The concern for me is that your general counsel sat before this committee under oath and was unaware at that time about any deadlocking.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: happening.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: However, there's ongoing litigation and that was not acknowledged in his response to me.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers cites Board of Correction recommendations on mandatory reporting, audits, training, discipline, and tracking lock-in duration. Chard says DOC has reporting obligations for emergency lock-ins and supervisors should observe and correct violations.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers asks which Board of Correction deadlocking safeguards DOC implemented

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: In a 2025 report, the Board of Correction recommended mandatory reporting of individualized and voluntary lock-ins, audits of logbooks,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: and surveillance footage, targeted staff training, discipline where appropriate, and track of lock-in duration and impact on services.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Which of these safeguards has Department of Correction implemented?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: So I know in general, when those allegations were made, again, we refer that immediately to DOI, and their investigation could not substantiate any of those allegations.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Nonetheless, at the time, there was communication and direction given from the top to the bottom that that is not within our policy, that's not something that should be occurring.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: The department already has reporting obligations related to emergency lock-ins, inclusive of duration and any interrupted services, so those reports have remained ongoing.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So essentially there are steps that DOC has implemented to be able to ensure that the staff understands that it's not permissible anymore through communication.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And how are you tracking whether or not it's happening or instances if it were to happen?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: That should be something that's being recognized by supervisors during their regular touring, because, again, it is not policy for that to be occurring.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: And so as supervisors and frontline staff are making their regular tours, that's something that should be observed and corrected for.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: And in the case that policy is being violated, of course, discipline is appropriate.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether DOC received additional allegations of deadlocking or involuntary individualized lock-ins in 2025 or 2026. Chard says DOC will have to follow up after the hearing.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers asks about new deadlocking allegations in 2025 and 2026

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Has the department received any additional allegations regarding deadlocking or involuntary individualized lock-ins in any housing unit in 2025 or 2026?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: We'd have to follow up with you on that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: While we're in the hearing, can someone just check and see if we can get that while we're here?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: We'll have to follow up and get that to you afterwards.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: I don't think that's something we'll be able to confirm right now.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers describes testimony that white tags were placed on cell door switchboards to indicate deadlocked individuals. She asks whether staff are permitted to tag buttons and what the tags mean; Chard says she is not familiar and will follow up.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers asks about white tags on cell door switchboards

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: In an October 2024 Board of Correction meeting, former Rikers Island social worker Justina

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Reswinski testified that correction officers placed white tags on the cell door switchboard, the panel that can unlock any door in the unit to indicate

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: quote-unquote deadlocked individuals.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: She alleged that this was the only record of deadlocking.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: In its closing memo for its investigation onto these claims, the Department of Investigation stated that it observed white

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: pieces of paper on eight different cell control buttons on the cell door switchboard in the control room.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Are staff permitted to tag cell door control buttons?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that policy.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: We would have to follow up.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: When you follow up, I'm going to just give some follow-up questions pertaining to that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So in the event that white paper tags are permitted, the question then becomes, correctional officers told the Board of Correction that white tags are used on cell door switchboards to indicate...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: That someone is outside of their cell at programming at court, but told the Department of Investigation investigators that white tags were used to indicate that the person in the cell had exhibited a certain type of behavior.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What is the purpose of white paper tags on the cell door panel?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And if white paper tags are not permitted, the follow-up question is, have any staff been disciplined for placing white tags on cell door switchboards?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Has DOC issued any memos or taken any other corrective actions regarding the placement of paper tags on cell door switchboards?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Can you confirm that these tags are no longer in use?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And have you conducted an audit to confirm that these tags are no longer in use?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I believe we have a letter that will follow this hearing to summarize everything I said so you know exactly what we're looking to get from you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'll pass it to Chair Frey.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I just have two quick follow-ups before I open it up for questions from members.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I do also want to acknowledge that we've been joined by Council Members Feliz and Santos Suoso.

chapters.summary: Farías asks whether CHS collects racial demographic data given the predominantly Black and Latina population. Merrill says race is not on the intake screening and historically has not informed treatment plans, though providers can ask if clinically indicated.
chapters.title: Chair Farías questions CHS on collecting racial demographic data

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: On the questions that Chair Brooks-Powers asked regarding

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: the racial demographic breakdowns of pregnant people in DOC custody, I understand that CHS's intake, from what I heard in response, doesn't collect that data.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: My question is around comprehensive health care.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: If we know consistently that the folks coming in for intake are going to be predominantly black women, Latinas, people of color,

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: when we're looking at comprehensive care, a continuity of comprehensive care, wouldn't that be helpful demographic information, helpful information to look at how we're holistically caring for a person within our custody?

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So we can always ask on an individual patient level if that's indicated.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: I think, as you said, the vast majority of women in our care are black and brown women, and we treat really every woman as

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: is requiring is a vulnerable population by virtue of being incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So that historically just hasn't been information that's informed treatment plans.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And there's no like intake form that you folks do where people self-identify?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: It's not one of the questions on our intake screening.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, so there is an intake screening form that we're checking off different questions, but that just isn't a part of it.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Farías asks if families are notified about the possibility of moving to the nursery. Greysock says DOC communicates directly with the person in care, and Colon says DOC generally does not contact family without consent.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks whether families are notified about nursery eligibility

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And then just another follow-up from a question that Chair Books Powers asked.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: For the notices regarding the nursery and potential eligibility on...

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Moving from general population to the nursery, have we thought through or are their families notified of the potentiality to move their housing?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Is that something that we've done in the past or we're interested in doing?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Because maybe sometimes encouragement is needed by family members.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Typically, we communicate directly to the person in our care, and they would communicate with a family member.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Yeah, generally, DOC is not in communication.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: We don't have a means of communicating.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And what about, like, counselors or the doulas?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Are those folks talking with family members?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Yeah, I think for...

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: For counselors or any of our DOC staff that are even or non-DOC staff or providers, we do often get consent from the person in our care if they would like us to reach out to anyone else, including their family.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Our social service team at the Rosam Singer Center does a lot of actually facilitated phone calls with a variety of folks from community care providers that may not be able to come on to Rikers Island and families as well,

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: as indicated and necessary.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: And so during those conversations, it could come up, the opportunity for the nursery.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: But since it is a consented conversation, we're not necessarily privileged to what that information or the case note would look like.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I would recommend just talking that through with doulas.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Sometimes you need your mom, your sister, your partner to tell you this might be best for the time being.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And sometimes folks don't want to feel isolated.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: They might think the nursery will be isolating, so they want to stay around other humans, which makes sense during a very traumatic experience being incarcerated and pregnant.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: But sometimes family support is helpful.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I will turn over to my colleagues for questions before I use the rest of my time.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So I'd like to first acknowledge Councilmember Morano, followed by Hudson for questions.

chapters.summary: Morano says it is extraordinary that babies live inside a jail and asks how many infants are currently and historically on Rikers. Colon says one infant currently and eight since 2022; Merrill says emergencies are transferred to Elmhurst.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano questions infants living in Rikers nursery

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you both chairs for highlighting such an important topic.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you all for your testimony and for being here.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony described the nursery at the Rose M.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Singer Center where eligible mothers can live with their babies until their child's first birthday.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I certainly understand the rationale for keeping mothers and infants together.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But there's something pretty extraordinary about the fact that New York City has babies living inside a jail.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I don't know that a lot of New Yorkers are totally aware of this.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So my question is.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many, just to follow up on what Chair Brooks-Powers was asking, but how many infants are currently living on Rikers Island, and how many have lived there over the past five years?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Currently, there is one infant, and since 2022, we have had eight infants.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What happens when one of those infants has a medical emergency?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is there a pediatrician on site around the clock, or does that baby have to be transported off of Rikers?

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So our clinical staff would respond to a medical emergency and then initiate a transfer to Elmhurst Hospital, which is also where babies receive their general routine care.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Has the city ever conducted an independent assessment of whether Rikers Island is an appropriate environment for an infant as opposed to some alternative secure setting that allows mother and child to remain together?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: I was going to say I actually can't speak on if there has been an assessment that's been facilitated.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: I think most importantly, what has been assessed is the importance of the parental bonding time and ensuring that we're offering bonding between the parent and the child.

chapters.summary: Morano asks whether DOC tracks incarcerated women who are primary caregivers of minor children. Colon says information is self-reported and not tracked in a database, but new intake asks about children and coordinates with ACS when needed.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano asks about incarcerated mothers' children and ACS coordination

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We're discussing women who are pregnant or who've recently given birth, but I think a lot of folks are also concerned about the children who were already at home when their mothers were incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Does DOC track how many incarcerated women are the primary caregivers of minor children, including children who may suddenly have no parent available to care for them?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: So our communication with the parent is one of self-report.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: So while we do maintain knowledge through consent of them sharing with us if they are a parent and the number of children that they have and the ages of their children, it is not something that is tracked via a database.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And do you coordinate with ACS or another agency to determine whether those children are safe or being properly cared for?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: While it's true that we don't track that information via a database, it is part of the new mission intake process to ask that question in order to assess whether there may be a child at home who has been left without care or otherwise

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: in such that we would need to coordinate with the Administration for Children's Services.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Could a mother be incarcerated in our city's jail system while nobody in city government has any idea where her young children are or who's looking after them?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Again, that is part of the new admission screening process on our end.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: That's a question that's asked.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Of course, if someone doesn't disclose, we wouldn't necessarily know that.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: But that is part of the question asked, and I would hope that a parent would provide that information so that their child can be cared for.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'll let, sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: I was just going to share and highlight that we have a team of DOC staff and also like a dedicated program specifically to support mothers and kind of encourage the mothers in our care to share that and get services.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: So, for example, we have a family visiting assistance program with our children, the Osborne Association, that provides that parenting support to everyone who is a mother.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: And so typically they share with us and there's ongoing support around visitation and child-friendly spaces and support for family members as well.

chapters.summary: Morano asks where maternity and nursery services will be located under the borough-based jail plan. Colon says they are slated for the Queens Detention Complex, with capacity around 450 while 482 women are currently in custody.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano asks where maternity and nursery services will go after Rikers

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'll end with this.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I have to ask about the city's plan to close Rikers Island because I think that's probably going to have ramifications across the board, including with respect to what we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We're talking today about a population with very specialized needs, and we've discussed maternity care, mental health treatment, a nursery, coordination with Elmhurst Hospital.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Under the borough-based jail plan, where exactly would the maternity and nursery services that are currently provided at the Rose M.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Singer Center be located?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: As mentioned, right now it is slated for the Queens Detention Complex.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: So that is where we are building.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But the capacity there would be, was it 482?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: We currently have 482 women in our care.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: It's approximately 450.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Recognizing Councilmember Hudson.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks whether medical personnel are consulted before restraints are applied to a pregnant person. Chard says restraints are used for imminent safety risk and may be applied without medical consultation, and medical providers cannot direct removal.
chapters.title: Council Member Hudson questions restraints and medical consultation

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask a few questions about restraints.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Are medical personnel consulted before restraints are applied to a pregnant person?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: I don't think we've had any specific incidents in recent history that I can call to mind, but I think generally what would be occurring is

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: someone who is kind of an imminent risk of harm against themselves or others.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: So in that case, if we are trying to prevent harm imminently,

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: and de-escalation and all that hasn't worked, then we would be applying the restraints directly to prevent harm immediately.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Without consulting a medical professional?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: In some cases.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then can a medical provider direct DOC personnel to remove constraints?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Restraints, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: I'm not aware, but I don't believe so because, again, the situations in which restraints would ever be contemplated would be, again, very rare and someone who is at immediate and kind of immense risk of harm,

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: as I noted previously.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: We're not waiting until we get to a certain location or a certain thing to happen to remove those restraints.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: As soon as a person is calm and it's safe to do so, the restraints are removed.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: So that we can prevent further harm.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And has DOC reviewed or revised its restraint policy in response to incidents, complaints, or recommendations from oversight agencies?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: I don't believe it's been revised in the past few years, although I'm not aware of specific complaints that we would have received that would have necessitated that.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Again, it's extremely rare that this would occur, and we don't have any incidents, I think, going back as far as six years.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks about annual pregnancy-related medical care expenditures. Merrill says CHS does not budget by diagnosis and most costs are staffing; a prenatal nurse position has been vacant for over a month and CHS is hiring.
chapters.title: Council Member Hudson asks about pregnancy-related medical expenditures and prenatal nurse vacancy

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What were the annual expenditures for pregnancy-related medical care for people in DOC custody in each of the past three fiscal years?

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So CHS doesn't budget by clinical condition or diagnosis, and we're not budgeting per patient.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: Rather, about 80% of our entire budget is devoted to staffing.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So most of the pregnancy-related care would be in direct patient services.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: And we do have an OBGYN and then a recently retired, although we're looking to fill a prenatal nurse position.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So those are really exclusively devoted to prenatal care.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: But in general, it's members of the staff from the mental health service, gender-related services team, pharmacy, medicine in general that are supporting that care.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And how long has that prenatal nurse position been vacant?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: It's greater than a month's time.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Greater than a month's time.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: And we're actively hiring.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What's the average time for hiring medical personnel, like positions like that, would you say?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Well, once we identify an individual, the onboarding process usually takes about, I would say, six to eight weeks.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: It's just a matter of interviewing and identifying the appropriate candidate.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And so are there, is that the only prenatal nurse position or are there others?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: We only have one prenatal nurse on staff.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, so no.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So there's currently no, everybody's going without a prenatal nurse.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: No, so let's not.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: There's a prenatal nurse line.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: However, there are other RNs that work in the environment that can fill that position until that line is filled.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: If needed.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks for annual doula program expenditures. Colon says the contract was approximately $200,000 over four years, averaging about $50,000 per year.
chapters.title: Council Member Hudson asks about doula program expenditures

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And what was the annual expenditure for the doula program in each of the past three fiscal years?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: So, sorry, I keep making that noise.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: So our contract was approximately $200,000 spanned over four years, so that averages to about $50,000 per year.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Thank you, chairs.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Farías asks DOC to verbalize and send the current written policy governing restraints on pregnant people. Chard says the policy aligns with state law and exists in general and pregnancy-specific policies, and will confer internally about sharing it.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks DOC to provide written restraint policy

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Just a question, some questions around restraints.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Can we verbalize the actual current written policy that's governing restraints on pregnant people and DOCs?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Can you give us the written policy?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: What is the current written policy?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Meaning what it's called?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: How it's framed?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: The verbiage?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: I believe that the verbiage generally is in alignment with the state law and the SCOC outlines.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: It occurs in a couple places, both in our general restraints policy, but also there is a specific policy in relation to pregnant and postpartum individuals, just so that it's clear and everyone receives the training regardless of where they're from.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Can you send us that policy after this so we can read it?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: I can confer internally.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

chapters.summary: Farías asks how DOC aggregates restraint data and whether incidents involving other agencies are excluded. Chard explains custody transfers to NYPD or OCA and says reports are generated by the agency handling the person at the time.
chapters.title: Chair Farías questions zero restraint reports and custody data

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So you folks have already stated that there's been, we have zero people that have been restrained in our custody, correct?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: We've submitted no reports within the past three years.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So I just want to, I'm just trying to like understand.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: How we're aggregating data around some of these things.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So let's say an inmate, someone that's incarcerated, not pregnant, just someone that's incarcerated, needs medical care, leaves DOC custody with NYPD to a hospital to receive a medical procedure.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Is that what happens when someone needs a medical procedure?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: When someone is in our care and in our custody, they remain in our custody throughout.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: DOC officers would be providing that escort.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So in the case where, I guess what I'm trying to figure out is,

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We understand from a case that we know of where someone was restrained or had restraints.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: They were technically in NYPD's custody, but they were still someone that was incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: I can't speak to an individual case.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: I'm not sure what's being referenced, but I do, you know, if you are, if we're discussing someone who's coming in pre-arrangement, there's custody transfers that occur throughout that.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Once someone has been remanded into DOC's custody, our staff are the ones that are transporting and maintaining custody of that individual.

chapters.summary: Farías cites a May 2026 case where a nine-month pregnant woman gave birth in a Brooklyn courtroom and asks why it is not in DOC data. Chard says the person may have been in NYPD or OCA custody, not DOC custody.
chapters.title: Chair Farías raises Brooklyn courtroom birth case and data accountability

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yeah, we have in May of 2026, a woman who was nine months pregnant gave birth in a Brooklyn courtroom.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I guess we have different reports on whether or not she was handcuffed during birth or post that.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I guess what I'm trying to understand is with our data, this is a person that was in a courtroom that was technically still incarcerated under DOC custody.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Why is that data point not a data point that you folks are referencing in your data?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Or is it that because they're in the courtroom and they're in NYPD custody, they're technically not on your...

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: On your data set?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: I don't know that that person was in our custody.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: I think generally speaking,

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Again, when someone's remanded into our care, they come into our custody.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: When someone has a court appearance, there is a point of transfer when someone's going into a courtroom, at which point OCA staff may take custody.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: But in this specific case, I'm not aware of kind of where they were in their court and legal proceeding.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: If someone's pre-arrangement.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: That person would not be in our custody.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: They would come in until after arraignment.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: If someone is going to a court appearance and they weren't in our custody prior to going, they're not in our custody.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: So if that person was in NYPD custody at that time, then that would be where the report would be generated from.

chapters.summary: Farías says she wants to understand whether DOC logs restraints when another agency takes custody during court or medical transport. Chard says each agency follows its own policies and reports, and Farías asks to discuss the specific case offline.
chapters.title: Chair Farías probes gaps when custody transfers between agencies

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I guess what I'm also trying to ask is, and...

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: That makes sense.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'd love to talk offline about this specific case so I can understand the points of whether it's someone that was transferred, someone that's pre-detained, all these different points to get a better idea on the case itself.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: What I'm trying to...

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Acknowledge or infer or figure out with you folks is if and when someone

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: is still under DOC's custody and another agency, whether that's EMS or NYPD or someone else might be taking, you know,

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: involved in an incident with them, whether it's in a courtroom or going to a medical facility, does that data set still end up on your side or is it expected that it would go to the other agency?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I say this, I'm only asking because there's times where we use these very specific moments as city government to kind of remove ourselves from accountability of that data point.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And so that's what I'm trying to get to.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: I think it's point of clarity.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: Pre-arrangement, someone is in NYPD custody.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So any...

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yes, that I know.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, like, so...

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: So what I will say is there's state policies, state laws that govern restraints on pregnant and postpartum individuals.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: They're overarching, but some of them are specific for certain agencies.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: So I think to the extent that someone is transferred into another agency's custody, they would be following their own policies in compliance with whatever laws and oversight is governing them.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Our specific policies are guided by state law and our state oversight bodies.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: And that's why we have those policies in place.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: That's where the reports are getting generated from in all those timelines.

chapters.summary: Farías asks whether someone can be transferred out of DOC custody and back in. Chard says chain of custody can occur with OCA escorts in court parts, which may create reporting distinctions.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks about chain of custody and reporting distinctions

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And there's never a moment where someone gets transferred out of your custody and then comes back in your custody?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: For any care, like any court date, anything like that.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: It is a chain of custody that can occur when someone's given over to OCA to do the escorting within the court parts.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: So that may be a distinction within reporting.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: But it's generally kind of associated with the staff that are handling the person in that moment.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Because those are the policies that would be applied.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yeah, I guess that's what I'm thinking.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And that's what I– we can continue the conversation offline, but that's the point that I'm getting to is, like, if we also use the data sets with the chain of custody.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: In parallel to one another, then that might mean DOC is not necessarily logging someone that's restrained or

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: shackled or handcuffed for a specific reason because they are no longer technically in their custody if they're given over to another city agent.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So that is like the point that I'm trying to get to.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: But again, I'm happy to specifically talk about this incident and continue talking about that offline.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Did you ask?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We've been joined by Councilmember Narcis.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'll pass it over to Councilmember Narcisse for some questions.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And thank you for being here.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks how soon after intake a pregnant woman is seen by an OBGYN. Nancy Farias says the goal is within a week, with appointment timing based on pregnancy status and clinical presentation.
chapters.title: Council Member Narcisse asks how soon pregnant women see an OBGYN

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: My, I think it's around the same question that Chair has, but before I get to that, I want to see how soon after intake a pregnant woman's person seen by OBGYN?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: So the goal is to see the individual within a week's time.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Within a week's time.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So I'm assuming within a week time, if the person is on what trimester?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The first trimester, second?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because I know in the ninth trimester, that's a little more kind of like you need a GYN to see that person right away.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: So then the GYN, upon the completion of the intake or review, when they get advised that there's a pregnant individual coming in, and then he, she, they will assign an appointment based on the determination of where that person is in their status of pregnancy.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Do you keep high-risk pregnancy?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Within the floors, how you address high risk.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because some folks are very, you know, have complications.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: So it's clinically indicated we have an infirmary, and if that individual needed to live there, they can do so.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: But we also have partners in Elmhurst Hospital, so if that individual needed to go, they can go there as well.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: That's where I work.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: On the presentation.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm used to be guys.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I used to work for MRS.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What happened when a pregnant person has a real high risk, right?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Does it manage her like right away?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Is that something part of the intake?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to get in my head.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Is it part of the intake process?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You are high risk, then you go to Elmer's Hospital or you go to a clinic setup.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: So the intake screening will happen at whatever time the individual arrives.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Then he, she, they will then be referred to the OBGYN.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: The provider that's doing the screening is also clinically competent to determine what the status of that patient is and make a determination if they need to transfer that patient to on-hurst.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Again, it depends on clinical presentation.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: Should they need to consult with our emergency response urgent care providers that are on island, they would also do that as well to get consultation and make a determination as to what to do for the patient.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So if that person from the outside had a physician that's following them, would you...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Collaborate with that person, do any calls made to see what is the complexity of that pregnancy?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: That is always the goal, to get as much collateral information as we possibly can from our patients.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: So the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Narcisse says legislation since 2009 prohibits shackling pregnant women and asks how many have given birth restrained. Chard says DOC has no such cases and describes intensive de-escalation before any last-resort restraints.
chapters.title: Council Member Narcisse asks about shackling and de-escalation

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Shackling.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We don't shackle pregnant women, do we?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Since 2009, we passed, there's legislation that passed.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many women in DOC or even NYPD custody have given birth while restrained since then?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Sure, thanks for the question.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Yeah, I can't speak for NYPD, but I do know that as far as DOC goes, there have been no women.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Good to hear.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: For instance,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If the person agitated, what kind of approach do you take?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: So in the case that someone is pregnant or is eight weeks postpartum and they're exhibiting concerning behaviors, obviously this is a challenging time and that can happen.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: Staff would engage in some pretty intensive de-escalation, trying to calm the individual down.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: There are additional staff members assigned explicitly so that restraints aren't utilized.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: It is really only as an absolute last resort when there is a situation that arises that imminent harm can come to the person or someone else.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: So at that point, it's a safety determination.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Cheers.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Council Member Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions before we move to the next panel.

chapters.summary: Farías asks whether the doula program working group meets every six months. Greysock says DOC participates at least twice yearly and has adopted recommendations on doula programs and support persons during birth.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks about doula working group meetings and recommendations

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: The city's administrative code created the dual program working group.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Under law, the working group is required to meet every six months.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Has it been meeting that frequently, more frequently, less frequently?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: We are part of the...

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: birth support working group.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: We meet at least, we join a group at least twice a year and it's been wonderful to be part of that group and get feedback and continue to work with our partners.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And what have been some of the recommendations the working group has made to DOC and have any of them been adopted?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: So in their recent report, they talked about ensuring that we have a doula program, which we have a really successful doula program.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: They talked about ensuring that we allow for a person to have a support person during birth, which is part of our policy and it's part of our process.

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: So we've continued to work with the group to make sure that all the recommendations are being implemented.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Is there a public place I can look at those recommendations or are those internal?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: The group has published the report, yes.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Would you mind sending that over?

utterances.speaker: Valerie Greysock
utterances.text: I believe it's publicly available.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll look for it, but it'd be nice if you have the direct link.

chapters.summary: Farías asks whether women are offered contraceptives before release and whether pregnant people can choose termination. Nancy Farias says reproductive health encounters include contraceptive options and positive pregnancy tests include options.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks CHS about contraceptives and pregnancy termination options

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And then for correctional health services, are women routinely offered the option to get a contraceptive, such as birth control, before release?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: So, yeah, at their reproductive health encounters, they would get offered.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Farias
utterances.text: So our patients get scheduled accordingly as well.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Do we offer all the options, like an IUD versus taking the pill versus the double shot?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: If there's a positive test for pregnancy at a screening, is the pregnant person given the option to terminate?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Great.

chapters.summary: Farías asks whether correctional officers are present during pregnant patient exams or labor. Merrill says mental health screening occurs during medical evaluation and referrals can be made by CHS, DOC, legal aid, or external parties.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks about officer presence during exams and mental health continuity

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Are correctional officers, sorry folks, got to ask all the questions.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I heard some.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Are correctional officers present in the room while a pregnant patient is being examined or in the hospital during labor and delivery?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And then my last questions, in case anyone else wants to think of any before we move on.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: What procedures are in place to ensure continuity of psychiatric care for patients who screen positive for depression, anxiety, postpartum depression, or other perinatal mental health conditions while in custody?

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So part of the comprehensive medical evaluation, the nurses, medical staff are screening for mental health needs, and then they can make the referral to the mental health service.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: As mentioned, we have a very low threshold for those referrals.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: And as mentioned, testimony, more than 80% of women in our care are enrolled in the mental health service.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: But referrals can be made at any point during the individual's incarceration from CHS staff, from a DOC officer, from a legal aid attorney, or other external parties.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'm passing it over to Chair Brooks-Powers.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks again whether medical personnel are consulted before restraints on a pregnant person. Chard says restraint decisions are safety determinations, not medical ones, made by staff observing imminent harm.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Are medical personnel consulted before restraints are applied to a pregnant person?

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: I think as I said previously, generally at the point, again, extremely rare in which we are contemplating restraints, that is a safety determination that's being made, not a medical one.

utterances.speaker: Chelsea Chard
utterances.text: And so the staff that are with the person who are observing that behavior, who have not been able to restrain or calm them down by other means, would be the ones who are applying the restraints and making that determination.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay, yeah, I wanted clarity on it.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: Okay, seeing no further questions, this panel is now excused.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We're going to call up the folks from Board of Correction to join us at the dais.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Is anyone else joining you at the dais?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'm turning it over to the committee clerk to swear you folks in.
