chapters.summary: Melissa Cintron Hernandez identifies herself as BOC Interim Executive Director and General Counsel, joined by Katrina Blackman and Chensi Augustin. She describes BOC's mandate to set and enforce minimum standards for care, custody, and safety in city jails.
chapters.title: Board of Correction Interim Executive Director introduces BOC oversight role

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Brooks-Powers, Chair Farias, and members of the New York City Council Committees on Criminal Justice and Women and Gender Equity.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to provide testimony on behalf of the New York City Board of Correction regarding maternal and mental health care.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: In city jails.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: I am Melissa Cintron Hernandez, BOC's Interim Executive Director and General Counsel.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: I am joined by Katrina Blackman, Assistant Executive Director of Monitoring, and Chensi Augustin, Director of Programming and Community Support.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: As an independent oversight body established pursuant to the New York City Charter, the board serves as a mechanism to keep our city's jail system accountable.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: The board establishes, monitors, and monitors the city's jail system.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: and enforces minimum standards governing the care, custody, and safety of people detained in New York City jails.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Oversight of maternal and mental health care is a vital part of this mandate.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: To carry it out, the board monitors not only compliance with its minimum standards through regular facility visits and inspections,

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: but also identifies trends and potential areas of improvement.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: The board conducts its investigations and system-wide reviews of critical issues, which encompass access to maternal and mental health care,

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: the delivery of services, conditions of confinement, and the systems intended to support the health and well-being of people in custody.

chapters.summary: Cintron Hernandez says maternal health requires services throughout pregnancy and postpartum and coordination during emergencies. BOC monitors facilities, advocates for nursery improvements, and recommends reviewing the nursery application process.
chapters.title: BOC describes maternal health oversight and nursery recommendations

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Maternal health involves more than the delivery of a healthy child.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: It must ensure that every person in custody receives the services to keep them and their child healthy throughout pregnancy and postpartum.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Correctional and healthcare staff must coordinate effectively and respond appropriately to maternal and mental health emergencies and ensure continuity of care.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Accordingly, the board must have access to reliable information that allows us to understand whether services are delivered as intended.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Maternal health in every phase is vital and should be regarded as a right of all individuals.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: The board has a productive partnership with the Department of Correction and Correctional Health Services on this particular topic, and we appreciate their efforts to address the needs of this population, including access to prenatal and special needs.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: individualized obstetric care, mental health screenings, psychiatric referrals, and individualized discharge planning.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: These efforts are particularly important given the mental health challenges that can arise while incarcerated during pregnancy and following childbirth, including postpartum depression,

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: anxiety, pregnancy loss, and separation from newborns.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: The board has dedicated staff who monitor facilities where people in custody are placed throughout their pregnancy and during the postpartum period.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: In the past, board staff have advocated for improvements to the nursery's recreation yard and safe and appropriate housing when the nursery was temporarily shut down for renovations.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Recognizing the importance of ensuring that those housed in the nursery or receiving postpartum care are produced for scheduled court appearances, we assess how DOC maintains appropriate child care arrangements for infants residing in the nursery.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Based on our observations of nursery operations throughout the years,

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: The Board recommends that DOC perform a comprehensive review of its policies regarding the nursery application process to accurately reflect current correctional procedures, including the 9 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Lock-in time and the discontinuation of the former punitive segregation designation.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: The Board also handles complaints from all people in custody.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Troubleshooting and resolving them one-on-one.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: From something as seemingly minor but not so as receiving a blanket, to ensuring crucial access to medical care,

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Guaranteeing that the board can continue this work is an essential component to maintaining the standards that are currently in place and continuing to be improved upon.

chapters.summary: Cintron Hernandez says studies show inconsistent maternal care in jails and adverse outcomes for children. She says BOC needs stronger monitoring and research capacity and supports alternatives to incarceration for expectant mothers.
chapters.title: BOC calls for stronger monitoring and alternatives to incarceration

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: For that reason, addressing maternal mental health care in the city's jails must also include strengthening the board's monitoring and research capacities.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Multiple studies performed in jail and prison settings across our country

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: have shown that conditions of confinement for people receiving maternal care are often inconsistent and insufficient, failing to meet the health care needs of this population.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: These same studies have highlighted how children born in custody have a propensity for adverse outcomes of preterm birth, low birth weight, and stillbirth.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: There are also numerous risk factors for morbidity and mortality during pregnancy and postpartum, such as a high prevalence of mental health conditions, chronic illness, substance use disorders, and limited access to health care.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Accordingly, there must also be a focus on exploring alternatives to incarceration that would allow expectant mothers to receive care in their communities.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Pregnancy and the postpartum period require constant access to medical supervision, mental health support, and opportunities to establish and maintain a bond between a mother and their child.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Alternatives to incarceration can help reduce disruptions to care and maintain connections to their families and community-based health care providers.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: The boards and its minimum standards of care play a key role in safeguarding access

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: and correspondence with loved ones, and creating opportunities to maintain family relationships and system support.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: As we continue to address the services available within correctional facilities, reducing the need for expecting a new parent to enter or remain in these settings could go a long way to preventing some of the adverse outcomes we are seeing in prisons and jails across the country.

chapters.summary: Cintron Hernandez says BOC supports a higher standard of care than outside jail, including immediate mental health access and a dedicated dormitory for pregnant people. She notes risks of general population such as chemical agents and lack of specialized beds.
chapters.title: BOC advocates for higher standard of care and dedicated pregnancy dormitory

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: To the extent that people in custody are in the care of the OC and CHS,

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: The board supports a higher standard of care than would be provided outside of the jail setting, given the serious factors that are at play in this environment.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: This should include immediate and consistent access to mental health services, particularly postpartum, and a dormitory where people in custody could reside during their pregnancy.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Prior to the creation of the Resch Annex to house men in the Rosam Singer Center, DOC designated a dormitory for pregnant women which allowed them to be cared for without the risks of being in general population.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Those risks are made evident with cases in which certain tactics, such as releasing chemical agents or other methods of control,

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: may need to be deployed in a housing area that would put a pregnant individual at risk.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: In addition, amenities such as specialized beds and other measures that are often used to provide better care during pregnancy are not generally available in general population.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: These, along with the rigors of daily jail life, can cause a cumulative effect.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: That results in detrimental outcomes and unnecessary stress for the expectant person in custody.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: The board's

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: supports the Council's efforts to bring greater attention to maternal health and believes this legislation provides an opportunity to build upon the ongoing work at CHS and DOC, officially implementing a policy for coordinated care from pregnancy

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: through the postpartum period.

chapters.summary: Cintron Hernandez says maternal health encompasses childbirth and the months after, requiring medical and mental health services, family contact, and continuity of care. She says BOC will oversee implementation and report concerns.
chapters.title: BOC concludes testimony on maternal health as a right

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: In conclusion, maternal health, particularly postpartum,

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: encompasses not just the immediacy of childbirth, but the months and sometimes years that follow.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Access to appropriate medical and mental health services, opportunities to maintain contact with their children and continuity of care, as well as coordination between correctional and healthcare staff are the pillars of maternal health that we should not only uphold,

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: but also guarantee through the policies in our correctional system in accordance with Section 306E of our standards.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: The Board commends ongoing efforts by the Department, CHS, and City Council to ensure availability and access to these resources.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: We are committed to overseeing the implementation of these policies and reporting any concerns to the relevant agencies, the Council, and the public.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Thank you again for the opportunity to testify, and we welcome any questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, and thank you for sending your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I had an opportunity to read it.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I appreciate the advanced opportunity.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether BOC has received complaints from pregnant or postpartum people. Cintron Hernandez says yes, including concerns about beds, healthy food, and access to medical and mental health care; Augustin describes women housed in general population during chemical agent incidents.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers asks BOC about complaints from pregnant and postpartum people

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Has the board ever received complaints from pregnant or postpartum people in care at the Department of Correction?

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Yes, we have a complaint line where people in custody can call with any issues, and we also have monitors in the facilities talking to all persons in custody, including people who are pregnant.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: We have received concerns recently.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: We went out, Director Augustine went out to speak to some of the people who are currently pregnant in custody, and they reported concerns about beds.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: About food, access to healthy food, routine access to medical and mental health care.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: And if there's anything else I'm missing, I can pass it over to Director, obviously.

utterances.speaker: Chensi Augustin
utterances.text: Good morning, good morning, Chair Brooks-Powers and Chair Farias.

utterances.speaker: Chensi Augustin
utterances.text: Yes, in speaking with a couple of the women, they did express concerns with being housed in general population.

utterances.speaker: Chensi Augustin
utterances.text: Two of those women, one while showering, the other while in her cell, were present during an incident and a chemical agent was used.

utterances.speaker: Chensi Augustin
utterances.text: And one of those women who was in that unit, was in the shower, also suffered from asthma.

utterances.speaker: Chensi Augustin
utterances.text: And so she expressed her concern with being in a general population house where

utterances.speaker: Chensi Augustin
utterances.text: the care and concern from the other women that she's housed with is concerning to her, where they're not generally concerned about the health of her child, but more so what's happening in the unit.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks about complaint trends and quantification. Blackman says numbers vary with census and stresses that a dedicated housing area would concentrate care and make it easier to identify and serve pregnant and parenting women.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers asks about trends and dedicated housing for pregnant people

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that, because as you heard earlier, I asked questions about this because I had requested that those who are pregnant be transferred into the nursery,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: only to hear that only one person has applied.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And so I'm curious.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: In terms of any trends you may have identified with some of the complaints from the pregnant or postpartum individuals in custody, and also if you can kind of quantify how many of the complaints

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: let's say in this year, you may have received from women who are pregnant or postpartum.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: Katrina Blackman, Assistant Executive Director for the New York City Board of Correction.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: So in terms of quantifying the amount of complaints we receive from pregnant and parenting individuals in custody, that number could vary depending on the census of those pregnant and parenting in custody.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: But as of recent, in preparation for and even before this testimony, as Director Augustine articulated, we do routinely tour Rose M.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: Singer, where females and pregnant and parenting women reside.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: One of the things that I can say in stress, and I think one of you pointed it out, which was really helpful,

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: is that having a dedicated housing area for pregnant and or parenting women would be extremely beneficial because then that concentrates the focus of care for those individuals.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: It can allow the doula, CHS, DOC staff to readily be available.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: To that population as opposed to, I want to say, for lack of a better term, touring around and trying to identify and locate where those individuals are housed in general population.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: I think having a dedicated location, it can also, without thinking too hard, you can add

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: actually know what the quantified number is if they're all in the same location, if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: No, absolutely, because when I went to visit and I wanted to talk to one of the pregnant individuals in custody, you know, we were on a hunt to try to find them and where they were at that moment.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: And I would also add the mental health benefits of being within a community of people who are going through the same thing you are.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: That can be extremely beneficial to these people.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: So we are really advocating for a space to be identified within roses.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: It doesn't have to be the nursery.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: It can be its own dormitory as it was before.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: For all pregnant people in custody.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks if BOC has analyzed the quality of services for pregnant or postpartum people. Cintron Hernandez says medical privacy limits full-scale analysis, but BOC monitors the nursery and addresses complaints.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers asks whether BOC analyzed quality of services

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And then have you ever done an analysis as to the quality of services offered to pregnant or postpartum people in Department of Correction custody?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And if so, what were the results?

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: So if we're talking about an analysis in terms of medical care, know that there are certain limits in wanting to do that in full scale.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: It will require, for example, access to information that is...

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Limited to us because of medical privacy laws.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: However, we do keep a close eye on those individuals.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: We keep a close eye on the nursery.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: We tour the nursery closely.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: We make sure that when people are out to their court appearances, that there's someone within DOC taking appropriate care of the child that is left behind.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: And we received any complaints about the nursery and addressed those.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: But I don't believe we received any complaints about the nursery conditions themselves recently, besides the rec yard that was damaged a few years ago.

chapters.summary: Farías asks whether BOC is aware of young adults ages 18 to 21 in pregnancy housing or the nursery. Augustin says she has not checked ages but would not be surprised, and notes pregnant women are housed in general population.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks BOC about young adults in pregnancy housing or nursery

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Are you folks aware of any young adults ages 18 to 21 housing any pregnancy housing or in the nursery program?

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: I'll pass that on to Director Augustine or AAD Gladman.

utterances.speaker: Chensi Augustin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Chensi Augustin
utterances.text: So to be honest, I haven't looked to see, to check the ages of the women who are pregnant within the facilities.

utterances.speaker: Chensi Augustin
utterances.text: I wouldn't be surprised if there are women who identify as being young adults and who are pregnant within the department's custody.

utterances.speaker: Chensi Augustin
utterances.text: What I find interesting, though, is that they're interviewing the women, as Chair Brooks-Powers mentioned, with having to find where these women are housed.

utterances.speaker: Chensi Augustin
utterances.text: Again, they're housed among general population, and the services that they're looking for, it's not necessarily as easy for them to access because they would technically have to leave the housing unit in order to get access to those services.

utterances.speaker: Chensi Augustin
utterances.text: But yeah, to answer the question in short, not 100% sure, but it is something that we can follow up on if necessary.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: We can follow up.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: We can check the ages of the people who are currently pregnant in custody and follow up.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I mean, I was also just going to see if the monthly census helps provide some of that data.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Whether that indicating we have young adults in either the nursery program or, but if not, it would be interesting for us to kind of start looking at that and pulling that data.

chapters.summary: Farías asks for BOC recommendations. Cintron Hernandez says the main recommendation is opening a dormitory for all pregnant people and reviewing the nursery application process to reduce intimidation and delays.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks BOC for recommendations to better support pregnant people

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Are there any recommendations for better supporting

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: pregnant and postpartum people in custody that you folks have or have been in front of and trying to navigate?

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Yes, the main one is the opening of the dormitory to house all pregnant people in custody.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: We are also advocating for the nursery application process to be reviewed.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: It does have outdated language, and we understand that it has to go through the necessary checks.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Checking criminal history, checking ACS history, but anything that can be done to expedite that process and to give resources to the people who are filling them out.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: We don't want people to be intimidated by the process of it, having to fill out so much paperwork.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: So having someone assist them would be very beneficial.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And is this a paper application or is this digital?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Paper.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Paper.

utterances.speaker: Chensi Augustin
utterances.text: And if I may add, the process is, as our ED shared, is not, it takes some time.

utterances.speaker: Chensi Augustin
utterances.text: In conversation with one of the women who did apply, I want to say she came into custody in July, and the application was finally approved last week.

utterances.speaker: Chensi Augustin
utterances.text: And so it does take time, even though, yes, it is voluntary, but there is a process.

utterances.speaker: Chensi Augustin
utterances.text: And there are other players within the process in order for it to get to that approval point.

chapters.summary: Farías asks for specific recommendations on expediting the nursery application. Cintron Hernandez suggests strict review deadlines; Blackman says the application has outdated language, redundant ACS questions, and literacy and language barriers.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks how nursery application can be expedited and simplified

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And do you folks have...

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: specific recommendations on how that process can either be expedited or made in layman's terms to make it more intuitive to complete.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I feel like, you know, sometimes with city government, generally we have applications that

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We have a lot of things we have to fill out and check out for our own data set, but they're not intuitive to a New Yorker that needs to just get through the process.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So just wondering if there are any specific portions of the application where you're saying this needs to be readapted or reframed.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: I can start off and pass it on to A.D.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Blackman.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: But one of the things that comes to mind is this is a panel that's reviewing these applications.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: So making sure that they have strict deadlines to comply with their review would be extremely helpful.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: And I'll pass it on to A.D.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Blackman for any other details.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: Yes, so when it comes to the application process, I want to say that, first and foremost, that it should absolutely be updated and reflective of today's information and language.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: And it should also, to E.D.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: Centron-Henaz's statement, that the interdisciplinary panel should be readily identified.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: Right now, part of the application process in terms of the language is outdated, and it speaks to the deputy warden of programs.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: But as we know right now, and tell me if I'm wrong, Director Augustine, there's now the executive director of programs that's at every facility.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: So that's part of it.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: And then when you review the application itself, the nursery application, I think some of the questions are a bit redundant, especially the part about ACS in terms of who lives outside of the home, how many children you have.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: And while all that information is important and relevant, I think maybe just having that question once during the application process.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: Anywhere in the application process is fine as opposed to reviewing it

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: or having to write it down a couple of times because we also have to be mindful of literacy.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: We also have to be mindful of language.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: English as a second language is also a thing, even though that the department has a very robust language bank.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: Some of this information might be a little bit exhausting when you have to write it out multiple times.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: If you've ever been to the DMV, you know what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And is this application in multiple languages?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Do you know?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: From what I could see, the application, I've seen the application in English and in Spanish.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Blackman
utterances.text: Those are the two languages I've seen it in before.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: And I just want to highlight that our minimum standards, 10-1-01,

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: requires that any communications of any significant matter provided to people in Class 3B in their preferred language, particularly if it's Spanish.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yeah, that's why I was asking.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Just wondering if we have a generated translated version and at least the top seven I think we have as a city, but we can find that out.

chapters.summary: Farías asks whether BOC rules adequately cover infant clothing and materials for children in the nursery. Cintron Hernandez says the rules do not address this and there is a gap in minimum standards that should be fixed.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks whether BOC rules cover infant clothing in nursery

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: After the hearing, just my last question.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: The board's rules require that clothing be provided to people in custody, but does not explicitly mention children who may be living with the incarcerated parent as part of the nursery program.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Do you think the rules adequately cover the necessary infant clothing and materials needed for the children that are with their parent in custody?

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: I can confirm that the rules don't go into that.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: I think there's definitely space to include that information, particularly in our Chapter 3, where we speak about pregnancy and postpartum care to ensure that any children who are in custody do have adequate clothing.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: So that is definitely a gap in our minimum standards that should be addressed.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I don't have any additional questions, Chair.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks what data BOC receives on pregnant and postpartum people. Cintron Hernandez says BOC receives a list of pregnant people in custody but medical privacy laws limit access to medical records, and expanded access would help oversight.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers asks what data BOC receives and needs for oversight

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Just a follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What data does the board receive on pregnant and postpartum people?

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: I'll pass it on to AED Blackman, but I do believe we receive a list of people who are currently in custody who are pregnant.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And what information would be useful for your oversight function as it pertains to pregnant and postpartum folks in custody?

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: So on the DOC side, while we currently have it, it's useful in terms of being able to identify where the person is so we can go speak to that individual.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: On the medical side, because of, again, the limitations that we have to medical information due to medical privacy laws,

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: if we want to do a whole-scale review of the kind of medical care that is given to this population, we will be limited in that.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: If we want to do one-on-one evaluations with the individuals that are currently in care, we would rely on consent.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: So that would certainly be of help to the board.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Our access to medical information is governed by the public health law and the mental hygiene law.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: There is currently a provision that allows us to have access to medical records of those who have died in custody.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: Expanding that, advocating to the state legislator to expand that access to encompass other types of medical information, particularly for vulnerable populations, will be extremely helpful.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'd like to acknowledge we've been joined by Councilmember Aldebar as well, but seeing no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So you do, Councilmember Narcisse?

chapters.title: Council Member Narcisse asks how many pregnant women are in custody

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: As now, how many pregnant women in custody right now do you know in DOC?

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: So there are five women who are either pregnant or receiving postpartum care, plus one mother and one child in the nursery.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So how many of them gave birth actually under welding custody last year?

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Cintron Hernandez
utterances.text: I'll pass it over to Director Augustine to see if he has the information, and if not, we will certainly follow up with an answer.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

chapters.summary: Hannah Mae Powers, health and safety policy analyst for Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso, supports Intro 902 and Resolutions 464 and 498. She cites high rates of perinatal mental health disorders and serious mental illness among incarcerated women.
chapters.title: Hannah Mae Powers testifies for Brooklyn Borough President on maternal mental health

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Hannah, you may begin when ready.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs Farias and Brooks Powers and all members of the committees for holding this hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: I am providing this testimony on behalf of Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: My name is Hannah Mae Powers, and I'm the office's health and safety policy analyst.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: Our office supports Intro 902 and the companion resolutions 464 and 498, which aim to provide more standardized and compassionate mental health care and processing for perinatal women.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: Maternal mental health disorders are remarkably common, affecting approximately one in every five perinatal women.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: Maternal mental health conditions such as perinatal mood and anxiety and substance use disorders are also leading contributors to pregnancy-associated deaths, both nationally and locally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: However, these disorders are not readily identified or adequately treated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: We also know that mental health disorders, including substance use disorders, are overrepresented among those involved in the criminal legal system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: This whole...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: It's true for women of reproductive age in the carceral population, with one study showing that 43% of them meet the lifetime criteria for serious mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: 53% meet the lifetime criteria for PTSD, and 82% meet the criteria for substance use disorder.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: Pre-existing mental health disorders also may precipitate involvement in the carceral system, especially for women.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: According to the Women's Center for Justice, over 80% of women in New York City jails have mental health concerns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Rikers functions as the largest mental health provider in the city, and detained persons with mental health concerns are implicated in an inhumane system that was not built to provide care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: We ask the council to reaffirm its commitment to providing comprehensive and compassionate health care to all New Yorkers by passing the legislation and resolutions on today's agenda.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: This will facilitate needed mental health treatment and allow reasonable considerations to be made in the criminal prosecution sentencing of perinatal and postpartum women in the crossroads system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mae Powers
utterances.text: Thank you again for the opportunity to testify today.

chapters.summary: Rachel Bronstein, Senior Director of Policy at Her Justice, supports Intro 1144 on gender-based violence data. She urges the city to include service provider and legal system data, not just law enforcement data, and to collect data on divorce proceedings.
chapters.title: Rachel Bronstein of Her Justice supports Intro 1144 and broader data collection

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You can just go down the line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Farias and Chair Brooks-Powers and the members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: My name is Rachel Bronstein.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: I'm the Senior Director of Policy at Her Justice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: For more than 30 years, Her Justice has partnered with women and gender-diverse New Yorkers living in poverty to address family, matrimonial, and immigration legal needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: Through our pro bono first model, recruiting and mentoring the city's premier law firms to represent our clients, we see firsthand how gender-based violence affects economic stability, health, and safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: Her Justice supports Intro 1144 and appreciates the Council's commitment to strengthening the City's understanding of gender-based violence through better data collection and reporting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: Our primary recommendation is that the City take an expansive view of what constitutes gender-based violence data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: Law enforcement data is important, but it captures only part of the picture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: Many survivors, particularly immigrants and others who may distrust or fear interaction with the criminal legal system, do not report abuse to law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: To understand the true scope of need, the city should incorporate data from service providers that work directly with survivors every day and the legal systems in which we work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: Legal service providers have valuable insight into the challenges survivors face and the support they need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: Our own data demonstrates that legal services can advance economic security and well-being.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: For example, securing child support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: can provide critical financial stability for families leaving abuse, and our research has shown that obtaining a work authorization improves immigrant survivors' health and stability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: We also encourage the city to collect and analyze data regarding survivors seeking divorce.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: As the Council moves forward with efforts to expand access to divorce representation for domestic violence survivors through Intro 1175, there is an important opportunity to address the significant data gap around domestic violence in divorce proceedings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: Better court data would help policymakers assess need, evaluate services, and inform future investments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Bronstein
utterances.text: Thank you for your leadership and the opportunity to testify.

chapters.summary: Jillian Modzeleski directs the Women's Defense Project at Brooklyn Defender Services and supports Resolution 497. She says no one should labor or give birth behind bars or in restraints and calls for trauma-informed gynecological care.
chapters.title: Jillian Modzeleski of Brooklyn Defender Services supports Resolution 497

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: My name is Jillian Majuleski, and I'm the director of the Women's Defense Project at Brooklyn Defender Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: Thank you to Chairs Brooks, Powers, and Farias for inviting us to testify today about maternal health in the criminal legal system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: Brooklyn Defender Services is a public defense office representing about 40,000 people in Brooklyn and Queens each year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: I helped launch the BDS's Women's Defense Project in 2020 after years of representing criminalized trafficking victims in the Human Trafficking Intervention Court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: Our interdisciplinary team of attorneys and social workers serve cisgender and transgender women who have experienced history of violence,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: exploitation, and abuse that has directly or indirectly led to their involvement in the criminal legal system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: In my practice, I have represented people who are pregnant, postpartum, parenting, and experiencing pregnancy loss, all while navigating the criminal legal system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: The vast majority of women with criminal legal system involvement have experienced violence or trauma in their lives prior to incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: Foremost, no one should be forced to labor or give birth behind bars, in restraints, or in a courtroom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: For New York to continue to subject people to these conditions is a devastating reflection of cruelty embedded in our carceral system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: All people in...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: The criminal legal system deserves to be treated with care, compassion, and dignity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: We strongly support Resolution 497 and are grateful that the State Senate and Assembly passed this critical legislation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: I'm looking at my time, and one point I do want to raise before my time is up is access to care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: Most of my clients have experienced some sort of sexual assault or violence, and that really prevents them from accessing care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: Gynecological exams can be very intimidating for those people, so it's important that the care that is provided for them in Rikers is trauma-informed around that point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Modzeleski
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

chapters.summary: Isabella Seda, Social Justice Community Organizer at New Hour, supports Resolution 497 without chapter amendments and Resolution 498. She also asks for broader postpartum diagnosis coverage and says health protocols should be established by health care professionals.
chapters.title: Isabella Seda of New Hour supports anti-shackling and court postponement resolutions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: My name is Isabella Seda, and I am the Social Justice Community Organizer at New Hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: We are deeply grateful for New York City's council members to address the impact of pregnancy on individuals in New York City's criminal legal system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: New Hour is a nonprofit dedicated to empowering justice-impacted women and families across states.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: We provide direct service to incarcerated, detained, pregnant, and postpartum individuals in New York and advocate for policy reforms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: We assent to the passage of Resolution 497, which would urge Governor Hochul to sign the anti-shackling bill into law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: We ask that no chapter amendments are made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: The experience of a mother who gave birth in shackles in a Brooklyn courtroom earlier this year and the injustice she endured has brought attention to the issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: But we recognize that this isn't a unique experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: Overwhelmingly, women are detained and pregnant and are constantly neglected and abused.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: Resolution 498 addresses the postponement to court proceedings for women in late-term pregnancy and early postpartum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: We have been able to see pregnant women subjected to lengthy waiting and holding cells.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: They should be able to appear in court without spending an often full day waiting in freezing cold cells.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: New York currently postpones court proceedings due to severe illness and medical injury, but not for pregnancy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: The same or virtual court options must be prioritized.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: We ask for the broader expansion of the approved diagnosis on postpartum on Resolution 464.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: Postpartum psychosis is one of the many possible...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: mental health challenges individuals face after birth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: Perinatal mood and anxiety disorders include a range of mental health conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: For those already sentenced, they must have the right to file a request for an alternative sentencing hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: Lastly, with reference to Intro 902, we believe that data collection is necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: However, New Hour has witnessed data weaponized against parents in family court proceedings and custody proceedings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: We acknowledge Intro Revolution 902 as an attempt to ensure transparency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: However, health protocols should be established and maintained by health care professionals, not the Department of Corrections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: We ask that City Council approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: You can finish.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: We ask that City Council approach legislation related to maternal health and incarceration with understanding of the challenges people face, rather than create levers of long-lasting negative impact on families, often already over-policed and targeted by misguided legislation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabella Seda
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Olivia Pickard, staff attorney with the Incarcerated Mothers Law Project at Volunteers of Legal Service, supports Intro 902. She describes postpartum clients separated from newborns and asked to sign away parental authority without counsel.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: Good morning, Chairs Farias and Brooks Powers, and thank you, Council Members, for the opportunity to speak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: My name is Olivia Pickard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: I am a staff attorney on the Vols Incarcerated Mothers Law Project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: Vols supports New Yorkers with comprehensive free legal advice, education, and representation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: For over 40 years, Vols has partnered with community-based organizations to provide free civil legal services to New Yorkers who otherwise would not have access to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: For more than 30 years, Vols Incarcerated Mothers Law Projects has helped individuals in New York's women's prisons and jails, including the Rose M.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: Singer Center on Rikers Island, with their family non-law needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: Through this work, Vols IMLP has provided legal support and advocacy to numerous pregnant and postpartum individuals in New York's prisons and jails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: Our pregnant and postpartum clients in jail or prison are at a uniquely vulnerable stage of their life, both medically and legally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: Parents often come to us with severe anxieties about the state of their parental rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: This is especially true for postpartum clients who may be separated from their newborn child soon after giving birth and do not know what to do next to strengthen or to preserve their parental rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: Many individuals in custody have experienced foster care themselves and are

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: are terrified of CPS, DSS, or ACS involvement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: In one case, a Vols IMLP client was separated from her newborn child immediately after birth by New York County DSS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: She was asked to sign parental authority away hours after giving birth without ever having spoken to a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: But perhaps the most visible issue is the toll on mental health of being pregnant, giving birth, and being postpartum while in state custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: Being pregnant or postpartum while in prison or jail can exacerbate existing mental health issues and often require specific and targeted mental health interventions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: Our pregnant and postpartum clients have expressed feeling dehumanized and traumatized by their experience of birth while in custody during a time where they already feel at risk of losing hope.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: Therefore, Volz IMLP strongly supports Councilmember Lee's proposed local law to amend the administrative code regarding mental health protocols for pregnant and postpartum individuals in the custody of DOC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Pickard
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Liz Swavola, Chief Impact Officer at WPA, supports anti-shackling and postpartum sentencing legislation. She says incarceration costs $500,000 per person at Rikers and urges investment in community-based care and closure of Rosie's.
chapters.title: Liz Swavola of Women's Prison Association urges community-based care and Rikers closure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: I'm Liz Suavola, Chief Impact Officer at the Women's Prison Association.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: For more than 180 years, WPA has served women impacted by incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: We provide a continuum of care with women in the community at Rikers Island and Bedford Hills and as they transition home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: Our work includes case management, alternatives to incarceration and pretrial detention, reentry, housing, and trauma-responsive clinical care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: We appreciate the urgent need to address maternal mental health for people in DOC custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: Pregnancy and the postpartum period are challenging and vulnerable times full of uncertainty and physical and emotional demands, all of which are exacerbated by incarceration and the trauma it inflicts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: WPA agrees that no person should be shackled while pregnant or postpartum, and that postpartum mental health struggles should be a mitigating factor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: We hope to see these pieces of legislation pass immediately.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: At the same time, we urge council members to work diligently to reduce the footprint of incarceration and close the Rose M.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: Singer Center, the jail for women at Rikers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: It costs a staggering $500,000 to incarcerate someone at Rikers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: Instead, those funds should be invested in helping women heal and thrive through community-based care and support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: Incarceration is not inevitable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: There are better pathways for women enmeshed in the criminal legal system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: including those who are pregnant and postpartum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: Incarcerated women are more likely to have histories of trauma, abuse, and mental health challenges that require access to treatment and care tailored to their unique needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: Research also shows that pregnant people often come into the system with experiences that can increase complications and adverse outcomes, such as poverty, being unhoused, chronic health conditions, and substance use disorders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: Jails and prisons are not equipped or designed to provide the necessary level of care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: The number of women incarcerated at Rikers recently surpassed 500, nearly double what it was five years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: While the number of men is decreasing, we are moving backwards when it comes to women.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Swavola
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ziyadah Touré Mateen, a member of the Cattell Center for Equity, Health, and Justice, says conditions at Rikers are dire and pregnant women need wraparound services. She urges the council to reduce the jail population and close Rikers, including Rosie's.
chapters.title: Ziyadah Touré Mateen calls for immediate Rikers closure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Salvina N.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: Brooks-Powers and Councilmember Amanda Forever for holding this joint hearing on the maternal health of the women detained in New York City jails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: My name is Ziadah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: I'm a tour mateen, and I am a member of the Cattell Center for Equity, Health, and Justice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: As someone who has had family members incarcerated at Rikers Island, I know firsthand how dire the conditions are there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: Every minute that passes by is another minute that the people detained there run the risk of losing their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: We submit this testimony to bring your attention to the ever-growing crisis at Rikers and the need to reduce the city jail's population and shutter the notorious and deadly jail complex.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: We are grateful to the council for introducing legislation that will require the Department of Correction in coordination with correctional health services to establish and maintain written protocol

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: related to the identification, screening, referral, monitoring, and follow-up care of pregnant or postpartum individuals with mental health needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: As a mother myself, I can confirm that pregnancy, postpartum recovery, and parenting do not stop at a jail gate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: And it is infuriating to know that women detained at Rikers are met with a system that fails to provide them with the wraparound services that they need to endure the health and that of their babies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: This system is perpetuating general trauma.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: I want to be clear that no city that is serious about reversing maternal mortality, particularly the daily

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: racial disparities that we face as black women, can continue to cage women on an island with a deep history of abuse and medical neglect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: The care they need is not getting delivered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: What is being done is simply putting a bandage on a wound that is far too deep and must be aggressively treated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: In this case, what the women need is an immediate closure of the Rikers Island Jail Complex, including the Rose M.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: Singer Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: These women should be in the community getting the care and support they deserve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: We urge these two committees and the full council to use their legislative power to reduce the jail population, advance the closure of Rikers with a clear

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: timeline, and hold the mayor accountable to the closure law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: Lives are at stake.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ziyadah Touré Mateen
utterances.text: Thank you for this testimony.

chapters.summary: Michael Tucker, with Community Hub and partner of Khalil's Cartel Center, asks the committee to audit DOC and CHS, freeze funding, and hold a hearing on Rikers Island. He says families are suffering and demands accountability.
chapters.title: Michael Tucker calls for Rikers hearing and audit of DOC and CHS

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: Good afternoon, committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: My name is Michael Tucker, not Khalil.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: I'm a part of an organization called the Community Hub and was invited to be a part of this as partner with the Khalil's Cartel Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: On June 10th, as well as June 25th, I spoke at the New York City Council of Criminal Justice hearings, representing a family who has a member on Records Island that's been there to date 3,000 days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: I'm here today because at both of those hearings, I urged the committee to do a few things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: One, do a full audit of Department of Corrections as well as CHS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: I asked that they funding be froze.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: To have an immediate, immediate hearing, if possible, at Records Island, because we're hearing from the people that work there, and it's come here to tell us what is going on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: When you ask them questions, they can't fully answer those questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: I would love...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: To see this committee hold this hearing at Records Island, to speak to the inmates, to the individuals that's there suffering every day,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: dealing with mental health issues, dealing with being abused by the correction officers and the people that are there in place to protect, not to protect them, but to basically make

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: make sure that they're doing what they're supposed to do in regards to doing their time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: Millions of dollars are being spent with these agencies, and they're doing nothing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: Once again, I'm asking that y'all have a hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: subpoena, the department, Stanley Richardson, have him come back and testify, the head of CHS, because it is critical that Records Island is closed, not tomorrow, today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: And people are tired of their family members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: Being suffering at records Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: And as I said, these are something, this is what y'all are here for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: And we're asking y'all to hold them accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Tucker
utterances.text: People are not being held accountable.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers thanks Tucker and says she has requested a hearing on Rikers Island but it has not been approved due to safety, security, and technology concerns. She says she continues to advocate for it.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers responds to request for Rikers hearing

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And actually just for the record, I have requested to have a hearing on Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it has not been approved, but we continue to try to advocate for it because there are a lot of layers in terms of facilitating a hearing on Rikers Island in terms of safety, security, and technology as well.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But thank you for all of your testimony.

chapters.summary: Farías sees no questions, excuses the panel, and calls Christopher Johnson for the last panel. She asks if there is virtual testimony and, seeing none, calls Johnson one more time.
chapters.title: Chair Farías excuses final panel and calls for remaining witnesses

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: See no questions.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: This panel is now excused.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I will call the last panel up for Christopher Johnson.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Council, do we have any virtual testimony?

chapters.summary: With no further witnesses or virtual testimony, Chair Farías adjourns the hearing.
chapters.title: Hearing adjourned

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Seeing no virtual testimony, calling one more time for Christopher Johnson in the room.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: With that, this hearing is now adjourned.

summary: Joint Committee on Women and Gender Equity and Criminal Justice hearing on maternal health and criminal justice, chaired by Amanda C. Farías and Selvena N. Brooks-Powers.

Testimony from Correctional Health Services, DOC, Board of Correction, Public Advocate, Council members, and public advocates covered pregnancy screening, prenatal and postpartum care, doula and nursery programs, restraints, mental health protocols, and borough-based jail planning.
Legislation discussed included Intro 902, Intro 1144, and Resolutions 464, 497, and 498; no votes were taken.
